paragraphs.text: Of Our Father among the Saints, the Bishop of Nyssa: First Book on the Inscriptions of the Psalms. O man of God, I received your command eagerly, since you give the same zeal to me as to yourself, and I have turned my attention to the inscriptions of the psalms. You commanded us to search out the meaning contained in them, so that what can guide us toward virtue through them might become clear to all. So, having studied the whole book of Psalms with closer attention, I thought it necessary not to begin the treatment with the inscriptions, but first to consider, with regard to the whole book together,
the aim of this scripture, and what it looks toward; and then [?] in due sequence toward the [?] … shows [?], and the order of the psalms toward the aim [?].

Chapter One. The goal of the virtuous life is blessedness. Everything achieved through earnest effort is directed toward some end. Medicine looks to health, and the aim of farming is to provide for life. In the same way, acquiring virtue looks to making the one who lives by it blessed. For this is the sum and the limit of everything we think of as good. What is truly and properly seen and conceived in this lofty notion may rightly be called the divine nature. The great Paul names God in this way, setting "blessed" before all the names given to God. In one of his letters he writes these very words: "The blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no human being has seen or can see; to him be honor and eternal might." In my view at least, all these lofty ideas about the Divine would serve as a definition of blessedness. If anyone were asked what blessedness is, he would not miss the pious answer if he followed Paul's words. He would say that what is called blessed properly and primarily is the nature that is beyond all things. Blessedness among human beings, through participation in what truly is, comes to be, and is called, in some measure what the nature of the thing shared in is. Therefore the definition of human blessedness is likeness to the Divine. The truly good, or rather what is beyond the good, is the only thing both blessed and naturally desirable, and everything that shares in it becomes blessed. So the divine scripture of the Psalms rightly shows us the way to it by a skillful and natural sequence. Its teaching appears simple and unadorned, yet it lays out in varied and manifold ways the method of acquiring blessedness. Even from the very first hymn we can form some idea of the matter before us. There the word divides virtue into three parts and attests blessedness to each part in fitting proportion. First it calls blessed the estrangement from evil, as the beginning

of the inclination toward the better. After this it blesses the study of lofty and more divine things, since this already produces a habit of the better. Then it blesses the likeness to the Divine that those being perfected achieve through these things, and it is for the sake of this likeness that the earlier stages are also called blessed. It hints at this likeness through the ever-flourishing tree, to which the life perfected through virtue is likened.

Chapter Two. We want to grasp more precisely the teaching about the virtues that the word sets forth throughout the guidance of the Psalms. So it would be good first to work out for ourselves, proceeding in order and sequence like a technical treatise, how the lover of such a life can come to live in virtue. In this way we would recognize the sequence of the teaching set before us. The one who intends to look toward virtue must first distinguish in his reasoning between the noble life and the blameworthy one. He must mark each with its own distinguishing signs, so that his account of them stays unconfused and is not muddied by anything they have in common. There may also be other signs of what is peculiar to each of these. But the more general ones, at least in my judgment, [?]

These things have now been distinguished in this way. Everything at odds with pleasure is hard for our nature to accept. By pleasure I mean the pleasure dear to the body, for the gladness of the soul is far removed from irrational and slavish self-indulgence. We have also already recognized the distinctive sign of each of the two lives, the life of virtue and the life of vice: vice flatters the senses of our flesh, while virtue becomes gladness of soul for those who achieve it. But some are only now being introduced to the higher life, and for them sense still seems to be the measure of the good. Their soul is not yet able to see the good clearly, since it is still untrained and unaccustomed to such contemplation. Toward anything we do not know, however good it may be, our desire stays unmoved. Where desire does not come first, no pleasure could arise from a thing we do not long for, since longing is the road to pleasure. So something of this kind must be devised for those who have not yet tasted pure and divine pleasure. Through it the teachings of virtue will be accepted along with something that gladdens the senses and sweetens them. Physicians commonly do the same: when a remedy is bitter and hard to take, they make it easy for the sick to swallow by mixing in the pleasant taste of honey. The introduction to the virtuous life has now been fully laid out in what has been said. First, the opposing ways of life must be separated from each other. Then each must be marked with its own distinguishing sign. After this, one must be praised in speech and the other made something to shun through censure. The mind must be strengthened toward each by the examples of notable men. Particular counsels must show the road that leads to the good and turn people away from the worse. And the austere and manly character of virtue must be made pleasant for those who are still infants, sweetened by something that gladdens our senses. If all this holds, it would be time to observe how, through the method we have considered, the whole teaching of the psalms has been set forth for us, keeping us from vice and [leading us] toward virtue [?].

Chapter Three. First, then, let us consider the device by which [the psalmist] made three things easy to take and sweet; we begin our inquiry from the last points. These were the virtuous way of life, which is so hard and strenuous, the enigmatic teaching of the mysteries, and the ineffable theology hidden in contemplations hard to reach. He made them so sweet that this teaching is eagerly pursued not only by per-

fect men, whose senses of the soul have already been purified. It has also become the treasured possession of the women's quarters. It gives children pleasure like a toy, and it serves the elderly as a staff and a rest. The cheerful person thinks the gift of this teaching is his own, and the one who is gloomy because of his circumstances supposes that this grace of scripture was given for him. Besides these, people traveling by land and by sea, or busy with sedentary crafts, count it a loss not to have this lofty teaching on their lips. In a word, so do all men and women in every pursuit, in health and in sickness. Even banquets and wedding celebrations now take up this philosophy as part of their merriment. I pass over the inspired hymns sung with these psalms in the all-night vigils, and the philosophy so eagerly pursued in them in the churches. What, then, is the device behind this ineffable and divine pleasure that the great David poured over his teachings, which made the lesson so welcome to human nature? Anyone might readily state why we study these things with pleasure. One might say that setting the words to melody is what lets us go through them with pleasure. But even if this is true, I say we must not pass it by unexamined. For the philosophy conveyed through melody seems to hint at something greater than most people think. What, then, do I mean? I once heard one of the wise discussing our nature. He said that man is a kind of small world, holding within himself everything that belongs to the great world. The ordering of the universe is a kind of musical harmony. It is tuned to itself in manifold and varied ways according to a certain order and rhythm. It sings in concord with itself and is never torn away from this symphony, even though we observe great differences among individual beings. Think of what happens with a plectrum that skillfully touches the strings and brings out a melody through a variety of notes. If the sound were the same in every case, no [melody] would have been formed [?]

[?] of all-wise motion, [and] has listened to them as they recount the glory of God who works these things in them. Truly, the concord of the whole creation with itself, blended from opposites, is a hymn offered in such a rhythm to the unattainable and ineffable glory of God. Rest and motion are opposed to each other, yet they are blended together in the nature of things. An inconceivable mixing of opposites is seen in them, so that stability shows itself in motion and perpetual motion in what does not move. All things in heaven are always moving. Some revolve in a circle together with the fixed sphere, and others unwind in the opposite direction through the planets. Yet the sequence among them always stands firm and remains the same. It never shifts from where it is to something new, but always holds the same course and remains in the same state. So the union of the stationary with the moving, always occurring in an ordered and unbroken harmony, is a kind of musical harmony. It produces a blended and divine hymn to the power that holds the universe together. It seems to me that the great David had heard this music when he said in one of the psalms that God is praised by all the other powers in heaven and by the light of the stars, by the sun and the moon, by the heavens of heavens and the water above the heavens, whatever he means by that water, and by everything on earth that creation contains. For the mutual concord and sympathy of all things, governed with order, beauty and sequence, is the first, archetypal and true music. The one who harmonizes the universe skillfully strikes it up, by the ineffable word of wisdom, through the things that are always coming into being in wisdom. The ordering of the world [?] is, then, a musical harmony, and God is its craftsman and maker, as the Apostle says. Man is a small world, and this same man has been made an imitation of the one who harmonized the world. If so, what reason perceives in the great world it will probably also see in the small one, for the part is surely of the same kind as the whole. Take a tiny fragment of glass: on its shining surface one can see the whole disk of the sun reflected as in a mirror, as far as the small surface allows. In the same way, in the small world, by which I mean human nature, we can see all the music that is contemplated in the universe. The part corresponds to the whole insofar as the part can contain the whole. This is shown by [?]

[?]. In nature there is no storehouse for the enjoyment people get in an instant, where they might store up for themselves the pleasure they pursue with such eagerness. Like a deceptive phantom, as soon as pleasure-lovers think they have grasped it, it vanishes and passes into nothing. Only one thing is left behind after such an apparition departs: shame. Shame stamps a deep, hard-to-erase mark on those it passes through. So it is possible, as in the hunter's art, to recognize the nature of the beast from its tracks. When the quarry is out of sight, hunters identify the animal by its track. If the boar or the lion gives itself away by its own tracks, it surely follows that the nature of pleasure is also known by the track it leaves behind. And its track is shame. So whatever stamps such a mark on the soul is either itself shame or a producer of shame. But we have considered this point only in passing. Our main task was to show, through the Psalms, what the end of each way of life is, the virtuous and the vicious. In the psalm mentioned earlier, he said that the end of virtue is peace and rest, a single-formed dwelling unmixed with the passions, achieved in the hope of sharing in God. There he indicated its opposite by silence. But in many places throughout the Psalms he cries out, saying: "But the lawless will be utterly destroyed, and the offspring of the ungodly will be utterly destroyed"; and, "Whoever loves injustice hates his own soul"; and, "He will rain snares upon sinners"; and countless others like these. The whole book of Psalms is full of praise for virtue and of accusation against those who live in vice. Its recollection of history is also divided between these two aims. Through people of good repute it makes virtue something to emulate, and through those condemned it makes wickedness something to flee. When it rouses you to virtue by example, it says: "Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who called on his name. They called on the Lord, and he answered them. He spoke to them in a pillar of cloud." But when it shows the evil end of vice, it recounts the sufferings of those condemned for wickedness: "The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. [?] burned up the sinners"; and, "Do to them as to Midian and to Sisera"; and, "Make their rulers

like Oreb and Zeeb and Zebah and Zalmunna, all their rulers"; and many other such passages. From beginning to end the Psalms cry out to you all their particular counsels. In no part do they leave out the turning toward the good or the means by which one may flee vice. All of these are joined to the maxims that lead toward the good. For to acquire the good is to flee its opposite and do away with it. It would be superfluous to set all this out in detail, since anyone who reads this scripture can see the zeal of the [?] for such things.

Chapter Five. The whole work of the Psalms is divided into five parts, and these parts show a skillful arrangement and division. The boundaries of the sections are plain, since each ends in the same way with certain divine doxologies. These can be recognized from the division of the psalms that we set out. The number of psalms in each section is as follows: the first has forty, the second thirty-one, the third seventeen, the fourth the same number, and the fifth forty-five. The first part, then, runs from the first psalm to the fortieth, which ends: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. So be it, so be it." The second runs to the seventy-first, whose end reads: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders. Blessed be the name of his glory forever, and to the ages of ages. The whole earth shall be filled with his glory. So be it, so be it." The third runs to the eighty-eighth, and it too comes to a similar close: "Blessed be the Lord forever. So be it, so be it." The fourth section ends at the hundred and fifth, whose close is like the others: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting, and all the people shall say, So be it, so be it." The fifth part runs from there to the last psalm, whose end is: "Let everything that has breath praise the Lord." Now it is time to say briefly what skillful order we have found in these sections. In the first, he stops those living in vice from their absurd error and draws them toward choosing the better. He wants them no longer to walk in the deceits of the ungodly, nor to stand deep in the evil path of sin, nor to practice vice as something fixed and settled in themselves. Instead they should join themselves to the divine law, having gained through meditation a path free from wandering. Then the habit of the better might take root in them like a plant,

watered by the divine teachings. The first entry into the good, then, is withdrawal from its opposites, and through this one comes to share in the better. But someone who has already tasted virtue and has come to know the nature of the good from his own experience no longer needs compulsion and admonition to pull him away from his attachment to vice and make him look to virtue. Instead he thirsts intensely for the better. The word likens the unrestrained intensity of desire to thirst. It sought out the thirstiest nature among the animals, so that the intensity of desire would be shown most clearly through the animal that is thirstiest of all. The animal it names is the deer, whose nature is to grow fat by eating venomous creatures. The juices of these creatures are hot and burning, and the deer that eats them [?] necessarily becomes drier, poisoned by their juice. That is why it longs for water so intensely, to cure the dryness that such food produces. Consider, then, the one who has been initiated into the life of virtue in the first part of the Psalms. He has come to know by taste the sweetness of what he longs for. He has consumed in himself every creeping kind of desire, and with the teeth of self-control he has devoured the passions instead of venomous beasts. He thirsts to share in God even more than the deer longs for springs of water. After such great thirst, whoever reaches the spring naturally draws as much water as his desire freely pulls in. Whoever has received what he longed for is filled with what he longed for. What has been filled is not emptied again, as happens with the satisfaction of the body, and the drink does not lie idle within him. Rather, the divine spring transforms the one who touches it into itself, in whomever it comes to be, and gives him a share in its own power.

Chapter Six. Now, the power and activity of overseeing all things belongs to the Godhead. So the one who has in himself what he longed for also becomes an overseer, and he examines the nature of things. That is why [the psalmist] made this the beginning of the third section of the Psalms, in which he examines this especially at the entrance [?].

…is called worse, and that, conversely, evil is counted among the better. For if justice is praised, yet the one devoted to it fares badly, while vice is reviled, yet grants to those devoted to it lasting enjoyment of everything people strive for, how can one not think vice preferable to virtue when choosing a way of life, the condemned thing to the praised one? So the man lofty in mind, stretching his eye toward distant things as though from some high lookout, saw where the difference between vice and virtue lies: that they are judged by the last things, not by present ones. For with the soul's overseeing and discerning eye he perceived, as though it were present, what is stored up in hope for the good. In his soul he passed beyond everything that appears, slipped inside the heavenly sanctuaries, and rebuked the poor judgment of those who meanly entrust the judging of the good to the senses. That is why he says, "For what have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired on earth?" In one and the same phrase he magnifies and exalts the heavenly with wonder, while with contempt and mockery he belittles and loathes what the eyes of the foolish strive for on earth. It is as if someone born in prison, judging the darkness to be some great good, had been raised and grown up in it, and then, having shared in the gift of the open air, condemned his former judgment, saying: "What sights of sun and stars, and of all the beauty of the heavens, I ranked below the familiar darkness, through inexperience of the better!" For this reason he condemns beforehand in his words his poor judgment about the good, saying that he was like a beast as long as he saw the good in those things. But when he came to be with God (and God is the Word), and was led to the right (and the Word becomes his guide on the right through counsel), and saw the glory in virtue, through which those who look toward heaven are taken up, then he uses those utterances, one of which regards the good in the heavens with wonder, while the other spits upon the worthlessness and vanity of the deluded zeal for this life. The whole passage runs thus: "I became like a beast before you," he says, signifying the irrational attachment to such things. Then he adds: "But I am continually with you." Having said this, he also adds the manner of union with God, so that we too may learn how one who was at first like a beast is afterward joined to God: "For you held my right hand," he says. By God's help he means the impulse of the mind toward the right. "And by your counsel you guided me"; for guidance toward the good does not happen without divine counsel. "And with glory you received me"; he sets glory over against shame. This glory, like

a kind of chariot and wing, belongs to the one taken up by the divine hand, whenever someone estranges himself from shameful deeds. And so to what had been said he added: "For what have I in heaven, and besides you what have I desired on earth?" This is what most people still do to this day: although such things are rightfully theirs in heaven, they nevertheless make it part of their prayer that God should grant them delusions born of fancy: some power, or honor, or wealth, or this wretched scrap of glory over which human nature has gone mad. But the one who has come to stand in those heavenly things adds in sequence: "But for me it is good to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord." He shows by this that whoever cleaves to God through hope in a certain way grows together with him and becomes one with him.

CHAPTER 7. Such, then, is the ascent to the height in the third section. The one who has been lifted up so far in mind now grasps the next step above and becomes greater and loftier than himself in the fourth part, passing, as it were, through a kind of third heaven, as Paul did, and becoming higher than the heights already traversed. For what follows is taken up no longer by the common man, but by one who now clings to God and is joined to him. Beginning the next part, the text says: "A prayer of Moses, the man of God." For this man is now such that he is no longer tutored by the law but becomes a lawgiver to others. Such was that lofty Moses of whom we hear: he who willingly shook off the royal dignity like dust clinging to the soles of his feet; he who for forty years exiled himself from the company of men and, living alone with himself alone, gazed in stillness and without distraction on the contemplation of invisible things; he who was afterward illumined by the ineffable light and loosed the foot of his soul from its covering of dead skin; he who crushed the Egyptian army and the tyrant with blow upon blow, but freed Israel from tyranny through light and water; he for whom, after Egypt, all time was one continuous day, the night never growing black with darkness. For after the sun's daily course another light from the cloud, newly devised, took over from the radiance of its rays. So although the sun set for them in its necessary cycle, the light remained continuous and unbroken, since the radiance of the pillar received the rays of the sun without any interval. He who sweetened the bitter, undrinkable water with wood, and turned the rock into

a spring for the thirsty; he who exchanged earthly food for heavenly; he who saw keenly in the divine darkness and beheld in it the Invisible; he who saw the tabernacle not made with hands and understood worthily the adornment of the priesthood; he who received the tablets made by God and, when they were broken, engraved them again; he who bore on his face the tokens of the divine power that had appeared to him, and with its radiance, as with beams of light, turned away the gaze of those who approached him unworthily; he who condemned by fire and by the opening of the earth those who rose up against the priesthood, and wiped out those who had insulted the divine grace; he who turned the sorcery of Balaam into piety. The end of his life is recorded as still more sublime: he went up to the summit of the mountain and left behind under the sun no trace and no memorial of earthly burden. He did not let time alter the stamp of his beauty, but preserved within changeable nature an unchanging constancy in the good. This is the one who leads us in the fourth ascent, and who lifts up with himself the one who has already become great through the three stages traversed before. For whoever reaches this height stands in a way on the border between changeable and unchangeable nature and mediates fittingly between the two extremes, bringing supplications to God for those who have been altered by sin, and conveying the mercy of the supreme authority to those who need mercy. Through this we may also learn that the further one withdraws from lowly and earthly things, the closer one draws to the nature that surpasses all understanding, and the more one imitates the Divine by doing good, doing what is proper to the divine nature: I mean doing good to everything that needs benefaction, to the extent that it lacks good. This, then, is the meaning I have grasped of this psalm, whose title is "A prayer of Moses, the man of God." Humanity had been overpowered by the evil of sin and, torn away from its union with the good, had become mixed up with the contrary passions. It needed someone to plead for it before the one able to recall it from destruction. So the man of God becomes its ambassador, pleading in defense of the fall of his kin and urging the Divine to take pity on the lost. For at once he argues his case, as it were, before the one who hears him, and says that to God alone belongs being firm and unmoved in every good and always the same, while humanity, subject to change and alteration, never remains in the same state, whether it rises toward the better or falls away from participation in the better. For this reason he asks that the Unchangeable become, in every generation, a refuge for the salvation of the one who wanders. Patrol. Gr. XLIV.

The passage runs thus: "Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation." Why does he say this? "Because you," he says, "are before creation, encompassing the whole extent of the ages, from the point where the nature of the age had its beginning to whatever end it will reach"—and the end of what has no end is infinity. "For before the mountains came to be," he says, "and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are." But humanity, through the changeableness of its nature, was brought down from the height of good things to the low and slippery ground of sin, and was dragged down. "So stretch out a hand," he says, "you who cannot fall, to the one who has slipped; become for us also what you are by nature," and "do not turn" him away from the height that is with you into the abasement of sin. Then he becomes the minister of the Master's voice and brings forward his loving words, saying: "For you also said, 'Return, sons of men.'" Such a saying is a doctrine; for the text looks to our nature and proposes the cure for its evils. "Since," he says, "being changeable, you flowed away from the good, use your changeableness again toward the good; and return to the very place from which you fell." So it lies in human choice to assign to oneself freely whatever one wishes, whether the good or the bad. What follows is another doctrine, for he says: "For a thousand years in your eyes, Lord, are like yesterday, which has passed; and the things they hold as nothing will be years." What, then, are we taught here as doctrine? That for one who through conversion has gone back again to the good, even if his life has been spotted with countless faults, so that the sum of his evils seems to amount to a thousand years, all this counts as nothing with God in the case of the one who has turned back. For the divine eye always sees the present and does not take account of the past; rather, God judges it as a single day or part of a night that has passed by and run its course. But present wickedness, even if sinners make light of it as nothing, is seen by God as a multitude of years. For he says: "The things they hold as nothing will be years." And he rightly and fittingly calls offenses "things held as nothing," because it is natural

that none of these things would be thought any evil by one who surveys human life. That is why he says that these are "things held as nothing," and that when they are present in the will of the one who does them and have not passed away, each of them is judged by the divine eye as a span of years. Again he sketches in his words the transience of our nature, so as to move God all the more to mercy. For he says, setting it vividly before our eyes by means of an image, what one should take the wretchedness of our nature to be: morning and evening, that is, youth and old age; green grass at dawn, then flower, then passing away. And after that, when the moisture of youth has been spent, the plant has lost its bloom, and its natural freshness has breathed away, dryness and withering are all that remain. For this is what the text says: "In the morning it would flower and pass away; in the evening it would fall, harden, and wither." That is human nature. In what follows he laments humanity still more, saying that the life of men has been consumed by anger, tossed about by the onset of wrath as by some wind. It is clear that by anger and wrath he signifies the activity that turns away, through which there comes a failing of [?] for men, and a disturbance of what was at peace. The passage runs thus: "We have failed in your anger, and in your wrath we were troubled." And to this he adds in sequence that it does not befit God to make human wickedness a spectacle, nor should our age, stained by our sins, appear before the undefiled face. He expresses this thought in these words: "You have set our iniquities before you." It is as if someone added "why?" to make the statement clearer, so that the meaning of the phrase is this: "It befits you to have good things before your eyes, but what is lawless is unworthy to be seen by you. Make humanity, then, such as to be worthy of your oversight, and let our age become worthy of appearing before you [?]; for as things now stand, 'all our days have failed.'" For not to be in you is not to be at all. Those over whom the dominion of anger prevails have a life without substance, like a shadow, resembling a spider's thread. For just as that thread is visible while it happens to hold together, but if someone puts out a hand, it comes apart at the touch of the fingers and vanishes, so too human life, forever entangled in insubstantial pursuits as in threads in the air, vainly weaves a web that does not exist. If someone takes hold of it with firm reasoning, the vain pursuit escapes his grasp and vanishes into nothing. For all the things that are sought after in this life

are opinion, not substance. Honor is opinion; so are rank, lineage, vanity, pomp, wealth, and all such things, on which the spiders of this life spend their care. For this reason such things need God to heal them. For I take this to be the meaning of the verse that says: "For the days of our years in them are seventy years; but if in strength, eighty years, and most of them are toil and trouble." It does not mean that life is laborious for one who lives beyond this measure, but that most of so short a life is spent in toil and trouble. Infancy is trouble; youth is toil; the middle of life abounds still more in troubles; and old age, above all by its very gray hairs and wrinkles, bears witness to an excess of toil. Again he devises another way by which the Divine might be reconciled to human beings. The sense of what is said is this: the mass of our sins draws on a great punishment, but the substance of our nature is so worthless that it cannot bear the anger our offenses deserve. Yet even if what is brought upon us as punishment is gentle, it will be enough to correct those who endure it. If, then, the gentleness of the requital has sufficed both for correction and for punishment, who will withstand the might of the anger? Or what number will be able to measure the terror of the wrath? If, then, the anger is unbearable, but the working of loving-kindness can be borne, "so make known to us your right hand," in a way we can bear, with correction worked in us by you in wisdom and not in punishment. Now that we have set out the sense beforehand, it would be fitting to bring forward the God-inspired words themselves, which run thus: "For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected. Who knows the might of your anger, and out of fear of you to number your wrath? So make known to me your right hand, and turn back those who are instructed in heart in wisdom." The phrase added next to what had been said is a fine one. For he says that, because of the weakness of our nature, we cannot bear the greatness of the anger that sin stirs up against us, but we need to be corrected. Let salvation through conversion correct us, rather than punishment for our sins. So then,

let there be joy in you [?] in place of the time spent in the humiliation of sin, and the years of wickedness are past. For this is how we understand: "in return for the days in which you humbled us, the years in which we saw evils." And so he takes courage, calling those enlightened through conversion children of God's works. For he says, "Look upon your servants and upon your works," pointing to the patriarchs, Abraham and those with him; for these are truly God's works. "And guide their sons." For those who do the works of Abraham become children of the patriarchs as well, adopted into kinship with them through virtue. Then in the closing verses he joins humanity to God through purity, praying that God's brightness may also flash upon our life through a pure way of living. "Let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us," he says, so that all the pursuits of our life may bear the fruit of salvation and all that we do may look to one goal. That is why, after saying in the plural, "And direct the works of our hands upon us," he gathers the many into one work and adds, "And direct the work of our hands." For the varied and manifold cultivation of the virtues becomes effective, and this is the salvation of the one who does what is right. In this way, at the fourth step of the ascent of the Psalms, the Prophet raised the minds of those climbing with him and set them above all the vanity the many strive for in this life, by showing that the cobweb-like and insubstantial deceit of material life leads those who pursue vanity to no good end.

CHAPTER 8. Next, through the fifth part, he brings to the highest step of contemplation, as to a summit, the one who is able to follow him to the height: the one who with a strong wing has flown through the tangled webs of worldly life. For those that are downy and frail, like flies with their weak and feeble flight, hover greedily around the sticky things of life and become entangled and bound, as in nets, by the threads of such things wrapped around them. I mean that they are wound about with luxuries, honors, glories, and all sorts of desires, as with spiders' webs, and become the prey and food of that beast who hunts by such means. But if someone with the nature of an eagle looks more keenly at the ray of light with the soul's unwavering eye, and, straining toward the height, comes near such webs, then by the mere breeze of his swift wings in the rush of his flight he sweeps away everything of that kind that he approaches, by the force of his wings. Taking such a one up with himself, the lofty Prophet (2) Perhaps φέρεσθαι. (7) Ed. ἑαυτῷ.

leads him to the summit of the fifth ascent, in which there is, as it were, the whole completion and summing up of human salvation. In the preceding part, through the voice of Moses, he reflected at length on the changeable and the unchangeable: the one always is what it is, while the other is always becoming what it is not. For this is what change is: the passage from what one is to what one is not. He showed that by the same power our nature freely flows away toward evil and is brought back again through conversion to the good, so that God's brightness can shine once more upon human life. Now he reveals in his words all the grace that has come to us from God, setting it in many ways before the eyes of those who look down from the height on the divine wonders. For he was not content to point out the grace in one way only. He depicts in various ways the misfortunes into which we fell through our inclination toward evil, and in many ways he recounts the help toward the good that came to us from God, so as to multiply the occasions for thanksgiving in proportion to the good things received, as thanksgiving to God multiplies as well. For right at the start he says: "Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever." Since "confession" is understood here as thanksgiving, not as the admission of sins, he bids us glorify God for his goodness alone. He signifies by this that all the good and saving things that have come to human beings from God have come entirely by grace and goodness, while we have supplied no reason for that good. On the contrary, though we had fallen into every kind of wickedness, he does not depart from his own nature but does what he is. For it was not fitting that one who is good by nature should work anything other than what he is by nature. "Let them say," he says, "the redeemed of the Lord, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy, and gathered them from the lands, from east and west, from north and sea." The text proclaims the complete return of the human race to the good. For in this word "redemption" signifies recall from captivity. And God gave himself as a ransom for those held fast by death, paying it to "the one who had the power of death"; and since all were in the prison of death, he clearly buys all of them out with the ransom, so that no one is left under the dominion of death after the

…without a share in the divine redemption. For it says, “From the east and the west, and from the north and the sea,” meaning the south by “sea.” So, having first set out in summary the kindness of God which he worked upon the whole of human nature, he next recounts in some detail both how humans flowed away into evil and how God led them by the hand toward the better in each case. He speaks thus: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place”—for they had left the way, it says. And the Way is the Lord. They wandered in the wilderness, outside God’s care; and this was all dry and parched, cut off from the spiritual dew. That is why, wandering in a land without roads, they could not find the city of God, in which the worthy have their dwelling. For it says that “they found no city to dwell in, hungry and thirsty”; for as their strength failed through lack of food, their trouble grew worse. How could there be food in a parched and barren land? And how could thirst be relieved in a waterless place? It is clear that the prophecy does not mean bread by food, nor water by drink, but by food the true food, and by drink that spiritual drink. The Lord becomes both of these, giving himself to those in need as each requires: he becomes food to the hungry and a spring to the thirsty. What, then, was found to end such helplessness—the wandering, the desolation, the misery in the waterless land, the fainting from hunger? O wonder! A single cry, turned back toward God, changed everything for the good. For it says, “They cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he brought them out of their distresses, and guided them on a straight way, to go on to a city to dwell in.” By “way” he means the Lord himself, from whom they had strayed. And this Way says in the Gospel, “No one [?] comes to me unless my Father wills to draw him.” That is why God leads those who have strayed onto the way. And this same one also becomes the city to dwell in, as the Apostle says: “In him we live and move and have our being.” Fittingly he adds the call to thanksgiving, that those who have received these things should “confess to the Lord his mercies, and his wonders to the children of men.” That is, let them not hide the benefit in silence through ingratitude, but proclaim the grace aloud in thanksgiving, because he has made full the soul that was empty of good things. For it says, “He satisfied the empty soul, and filled the hungry soul with good things.” Again, in another way, he brings before our eyes the misfortune of our nature and recounts the divine love for humanity

by which nature is refashioned for the better. What he says is this: that humankind turned away from the light, sank down toward sin, no longer stood upright, and was estranged from the true life. For it says, “Sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron.” For it could not move away from evil, held fast by the heavy fetter. And the fetter is poverty of the good, like iron molded around the heart. The cause of all this was disobedience to the divine law and the rejection of the counsel of the Most High. This is what he means when he says, “Because they embittered the words of God and provoked the counsel of the Most High.” As a consequence, naturally, toil and humiliation take hold of the life of such people: toil because they were cut off from their food, humiliation because they did not wish to remain in the Most High. For it says, “Their heart was humbled with toils.” To be cut off from strength is nothing other than weakness; for who without strength could find help? Therefore he says, “They grew weak, and there was none to help.” But again a single cry turned their misfortunes into gladness. For it says, “They cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he saved them out of their distresses.” He does away with the darkness, abolishes death, breaks the bonds. For it says, “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds apart.” So let the grace be proclaimed with praise, it says, because death’s inescapable prison has been broken open—the prison secured with bronze gates and iron bars, as the prophet says. For such was the strength of death thought to be, until the power of death was abolished by the coming of the true Life: whatever came inside it remained there with no escape, as if held by iron bars and gates never opened. But “he shattered,” it says, “bronze gates, and crushed iron bars.” This means doing away with the way of their lawlessness and reshaping their life toward godliness. The destruction of those gates is the refashioning of life toward righteousness. For it says, “He took hold of them, out of the way of their lawlessness.” Again he presents human wretchedness in another way. The thought he expresses is that lawlessness is humiliation. And he says so rightly, for the word of another prophet agrees with this idea, saying that “lawlessness sits upon a talent of lead.” He shows that evil is heavy and drags downward, and that the one who stands on high through likeness to the Divine is pulled down by it into its own

pit. For it says that “because of their lawless deeds they were humbled.” And for this reason they turned away from that all-sufficient food of which the word said to the first humans, “Of every tree in paradise you shall eat for food.” For as there it calls the fullness of every good “every tree,” so here the word calls the true and all-sufficient food “all food”; to turn away from it brings on the weakness that ends in death. He says thus: “Their soul loathed all food, and they drew near to the gates of death.” And again a cry to God turns misfortune into festival. For it says, “They cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he saved them out of their distresses.” And he describes the manner of their salvation; the description is plainly the Gospel. For it says, “He sent his Word, and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions.” You see a living and ensouled Word sent for the salvation of the perishing, rescuing from corruption the one who had fallen into it. What evangelist proclaims the mystery so openly? So let the grace be praised, it says, by those who have been treated well, and let their praise become a hymn for the benefits received. For it says, “Let them offer him a sacrifice of praise, and declare his works with rejoicing.” After this he again describes the sufferings, and again, after the sufferings, brings in the grace of God. He speaks of human folly: that leaving the stable, unruffled life, they chose to take to the open sea. For it says, “Those who go down to the sea in ships”—and instead of tilling paradise, where they had first been placed, they made their work under the water. By “sea” he means this material life, stirred by all the winds of temptation and heaving with passion upon passion. For it says, “doing business in many waters.” And “they saw the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.” For having sunk into the depths of a wicked life, and often suffering the evil shipwrecks of the soul, they saw in their own case the works of love for humanity of the one who rescued us from the depths. For it says, “He spoke, and a stormy wind arose.” This thought must be referred not to God but to the enemy. For it is the voice of the adversary that produces the “stormy wind.” A tempest is a violent wind that does not strike straight on but whirls around itself in a sharp eddy; and when it falls violently on the water, it is as though some

great rock had been hurled in: the sea, pressed down by the weight, is split apart by the force of the wind wherever the wind comes crashing down, and the impact of the weight spurts the water upward on this side and that. Therefore he adds, vividly depicting the terrors, that the moment the stormy wind struck, “the waves” of the sea “were lifted up, rising to the heavens and sinking down to the depths.” For truly the rising of such waves to the heights—I mean the waves of the passions—becomes the cause of the descent into the abyss. And we have learned from many places in Scripture that the abyss is the dwelling of the demons. Those swamped by this turmoil and the tossing of the waves lose their senses from dizziness, their heads heavy, as if drunk, with the sickness of such a voyage. For it says, “They were troubled and staggered like a drunkard.” And once out of their senses, they can find no plan for safety; their wisdom is shipwrecked and lost before they are. Therefore he says that “all their wisdom was swallowed up.” And again, even when these are in such great evils, the way out of this helpless misery is the cry to the Divine. For it says, “They cried to the Lord in their affliction, and he brought them out of their distresses.” And at once the tempest was changed into a favorable wind for sailing, and the sea, its waves laid low, grows calm and quiet. For it says, “He turned the tempest into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.” Perhaps by the word “silence” he indicates that the waves are certain powers possessed of free choice, by which he points to the apostate nature, to which the Lord said in the Gospel, “Be silent! Be muzzled!” By “breeze” he means the grace of the Spirit, which by spiritual sails brings the soul to anchor in the divine harbor, the Word steering and directing it on its voyage. For it says, “He guided them to the harbor they desired.” After this he again bids both people and Church sing the praise of grace, all but sketching in his words the present state of the Churches: that from the seat of those who preside over the word these wonders of God are proclaimed, through which the faith, firm…

…the inflows of streams and the courses of water, meaning the successions of evils: when people, forever joining wickedness to wickedness, draw out the trail of evil like a stream. But also “a fruitful land,” it says, “he made into salt”; for the soul once fertile in evils was transformed and became thirsty, seasoned with the divine salt of teaching, so that the evil of those dwelling there no longer grows, fed by wicked inflows of water. And the salty and thirsty soul, which has taken up the blessed thirst, becomes a lake, spreading out like a sea with the gathering of the virtues. For it says, “He turned the desert into pools of water, and a waterless land into courses of water.” This becomes a city, inhabited by those who thirst for righteousness. For no one who is nauseated and has no appetite comes to live beside such a lake and such waters, bringing with him a soul glutted with evil. “And they sow fields and plant vineyards.” By such riddles he indicates the divine commandments and the virtuous way of life. For the commandment is the seed of the fruit to come. And virtue is the vine that, through its rational clusters, pours out the wine into the bowl of wisdom. These are nothing other than an abundance of blessing. For it says, “He blessed them, and they multiplied greatly, and he did not let their cattle decrease.” By “cattle” he means the obedient service of the soul’s impulses, when each of the faculties within us is put to use for virtue. Anger is a good beast when it becomes the yoke-animal of reason; another such beast is desire, carrying the soul on its back, as it were, bearing it up and leading it to the heights, when it is steered upward by the rein of the mind. And all the others too are beasts increased by the blessing, when they serve us toward great things. Then in what follows he makes a summary of all that has been said. For having gone through the sufferings in many ways and set the divine benefits before our eyes, he now gathers them up again briefly and sums them up in his words, where he says, “They became few and were afflicted by the oppression of evils and pain.” By “few” he indicates smallness, and the shrinking from height and greatness down to lowliness; for “few” means, in sense, the very smallest. By “affliction” he means kinship with evil. And by “oppression and pain” he everywhere means the end result of falling away from good things, as he explains such a thing in another psalm, saying, “The pangs of death surrounded me, the dangers of Hades found me; I found oppression and pain.” Having called sins the pangs of death and the dangers of Hades, he adds the end in which the nature of sin terminates, which is nothing other than oppression and pain; just as the Gospel, through “weeping and gnashing [?]

of teeth,” indicates this very same thing. Then he adds, in sequence, “And nothingness was poured out upon rulers.” Through these words he teaches that to be in what truly is, is truly to be. But if someone has fallen away from what is, he is not in being either. For to be in evil is not, properly speaking, to be. For evil does not exist in and of itself; rather, the absence of the good becomes evil. So, just as the one who is in what is has being, so the one who has come to be in nothing (and that is evil) has been “nothinged,” as the word puts it. Such a use of words is quite worn and familiar in ordinary speech. Just as we say that food which has turned into flesh is “enfleshed,” and wine poured into water is “watered down,” and iron in the fire is “set afire,” so too the one who has fallen from what is and come to be in nothing is “nothinged.” So “nothingness” is the absence of being in the good. And this, coming upon the rulers of evil—that is, upon the first humans—was poured out like a foul stream upon the succession of those born after them. Since, then, nature became poor of such a possession—I mean life—and man was made poor by the thief, robbed of the divine blessing, he therefore says that “he helped the poor man out of poverty.” For by his poverty we became rich. And the good shepherd made them, instead of beasts, “sheep of families.” He calls “family” the company of those who belong to the divine register, as the Apostle also says: “from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.” Then he adds that “the upright will see and be afraid,” teaching by these words that the upright man, seeing this love for humanity, should fear. For fear is no small safeguard of good things, bringing the one who has suffered to his senses for the future by the memory of what has happened. And when fear prevails [?] and drives out of us all the readiness for evil that comes from slackness, “all lawlessness,” it says, “will stop its mouth.” How blessed is that life in which the mouth of lawlessness, like a spring of mud, is stopped forever! [?]

…the adversary, that state will receive us for which no word will be found able to describe it, and which has been testified by the divine voice to be beyond sense and knowledge. To these things he adds, like a seal, the closing words, saying, “Who is wise and will keep these things, and they will understand the mercies of the Lord?” For since the activity of wisdom is twofold—one part searching out and seeking what is beneficial, the other guarding what has been found—he wishes the one work of wisdom, I mean seeking, to cease at that time. For what use will we have for seeking when what we sought is present? He bids only the one remaining work to be done: that the good we have gained be guarded, with wisdom working with us toward this. And what is this wisdom, and what is the guarding of good things? Not to be without understanding of the divine love for humanity. For the one who understands what he has received would not throw away the good of which he has been found worthy. But the one who has no understanding of grace will suffer the same as the blind, who, taking a pearl or an emerald or some other precious stone in their hands, throw it away like a worthless pebble, losing the possession against their will through ignorance of its beauty.

CHAPTER [?]. As for these five divisions of the Psalms, which we have perceived as steps rising one above another in a certain ordered sequence, we have distinguished them by the signs mentioned: namely, that the final utterance of each section forms a kind of pause in the discourse and a resting-point for the thought, enclosing within itself the conclusion of what went before, through the doxological and thankful words that say, “Blessed be the Lord forever. So be it, so be it.” The meaning of these words is a thanksgiving that endures forever; for the word did not end the blessing by saying “So be it” only once, but by repeating the word twice it establishes everlastingness in thanksgiving as a law. And in each of the parts divided according to these sections, the word has contemplated some particular good through which blessedness comes to us from God, following a certain ordered sequence of the goods contemplated in each, always lifting the soul to what is higher, until it reaches the highest of goods. And this is the praise of God fulfilled in all the saints, as the last psalm has it, saying, “Praise God in his saints.” There “the firmament of his power” signifies unchangeableness in the good, and “the mighty deeds of God” indicate that [?] nature

is no longer under the dominion of evil. Then at last human power is able to make its praise according to the abundance of his greatness, no longer uttering small things, but now surpassing the trumpets in loudness. For it says, “Praise the Lord with the sound of the trumpet.” Then it also imitates the harmony of the universe through the rich variety of the virtues, becoming an instrument for God in the rhythm of melody. The word calls this, by a figurative meaning, “psaltery and lyre.” After this, laying aside everything earthy, dull and voiceless, it joins the sound of its own strings, in the loud voice of the drums, to the heavenly dances. The strings stretched on the instrument would be that quality in each virtue which never yields or slackens toward evil. Through these comes the fine concert of the cymbal blending with the strings, when the sound of the cymbals stirs up eagerness for the divine choir. This seems to me to express the union of our nature with the angels, where it says, “Praise the Lord with well-sounding cymbals.” For such a meeting—I mean of the angelic with the human—when human nature is brought back to its ancient lot, will produce that sweet sound of thanksgiving through their striking against one another; and through one another and with one another they will forever hymn the thanksgiving offered to God for his love for humanity. This is what the meeting of cymbal with cymbal indicates. One cymbal is the supramundane nature of the angels; the other cymbal is the rational creation of humans. But sin separated the one from the other. So when God’s love for humanity joins both together again, then the two, united with one another, will sound out that praise, as the great Apostle also says: “Every tongue shall confess, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” When this happens, the sound of these cymbals will raise a shout of victory, arising through their common harmony at the destruction of the Enemy. And when he has been utterly destroyed and has passed into non-existence, the praise of God will be fulfilled unceasingly and forever in every breath, with equal honor. For since “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner,” and there will then be no sinner, because sin will no longer exist, every breath forever

…of wisdom has been shown to us, always leading those who are guided by these things toward the height on to what is greater and loftier in the life of virtue, so that one may arrive at that measure of blessedness beyond which the mind cannot reach by any conjectures and surmises, nor can reason discover by logical sequence what lies further on. Even the movement of hope, which everywhere leaps ahead of our desire and runs before it, stands idle once it draws near to what cannot be imagined. What lies beyond this is better than anything hope can reach. The philosophy of the psalter itself bears witness to this through the order we have considered. At the very beginning of its words it opens for us, as a kind of door and entrance to the blessed life, the withdrawal from evil. For this is what the first words of the psalter teach, when they say that the beginning of blessedness is estrangement from evil. Then it offers the guidance of the law to those who are going astray, promises that through such a life they will become like the ever-flourishing tree, and shows the grim lot of those who turn to the opposite way; and so, by successive ascents, it leads the one who follows this guidance to the summit of blessedness. For this is what the meaning of the last psalm shows you. There, after evil has been utterly destroyed, everything that exists will be holy, and all things will join in harmony in the praise of God. All alike will have gained, in the firmament of his power, an immovability toward evil, and will lift up together a sound of praise to his majesty as though on a loud-voiced trumpet. When the whole creation is joined into a single choir, all that is above and all that is below, then the intelligible creation, like a cymbal, together with the creation now divided and separated by sin, will produce the good sound out of our harmony. When what is ours joins with what is angelic, and the divine battle line, recovering itself from confusion, raises the shout of victory to the Victor over the slaughter of the enemies, then comes the praise of every breath. It prolongs grace forever and, ever increasing, abounds into unending [?] blessedness. I mean that truly blessed state in which the mind that conjectures after knowledge stands idle, and our activity of hoping stands idle too. In their place comes a state that is ineffable and incomprehensible and better than all thought, which 'eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has the human heart contained.' For this is how the divine Apostle defined the good things laid up in sanctification.

Since, then, the phrase 'For the end' is written at the head of most of the psalms, I think we ought to understand it in the sense made clear by the other translators of the same Scripture. For one of them, instead of 'For the end', says 'To the one who gives victory'; another, 'A song of victory'; another, 'For victory'. Now victory is the end of every contest, and it is with their eyes on victory that those who strip for the games take up the struggle. So it seems to me that by 'the end' the word, in a brief phrase, rouses to eagerness those who, through virtue, compete in the stadium of life [?]…

[?] athlete… It signifies the choral dance that awaits us after the end of our labours; for this is how the word has been explained by the other translators, who render 'Maeleth' as 'with dancing'. And the word helps us to look to the hidden things; to make our song for the beloved; to sing for the morning help; to keep the Eighth before our eyes; to look to her who inherits; to place ourselves outside all kinship with Korah; and to have engraved, as on a pillar in each one's soul as a model of forbearance, that great utterance of David, 'Do not destroy', which he spoke to his shield-bearer when he was rushing to kill Saul. And anyone who examines all such phrases carefully will find that they are athletic exhortations called out by the trainer to the athletes, so that one may reach the goal of victory. In the same way, if any piece of history is written alongside the phrase 'For the end', it looks to this very purpose: that by historical examples we may be strengthened all the more for the contests. This, then, is the meaning of 'For the end'.

CHAPTER 3. Psalm, song, praise, hymn and prayer differ from one another as follows. A psalm is the melody produced by a musical instrument; a song is the utterance of the melody by the mouth, together with the words. Prayer is a supplication brought to God about something beneficial. A hymn is the praise offered to God for the good things we already have. Praise (whether called *ainos* or *ainesis*, for both mean the same thing) contains the praising of the divine wonders; for *epainos* is nothing other than an intensified *ainos*. Often these terms are linked together in the inscriptions in a kind of pairing, so that by the combination the two become one: 'A psalm of a song', or 'A song of a psalm', or 'A psalm in hymns', or, as we have learned in Habakkuk, 'A prayer with a song'. The meaning by which these inscriptions guide us toward virtue is this. The psaltery is a musical instrument that produces its sound from the upper parts of its frame, and the music of such an instrument is called a psalm. So the word that exhorts us to virtue draws its point from the shape of the instrument's construction. It urges that your life be a psalm: not one that resounds with earthly sounds (by sounds I mean thoughts), but one that produces a pure and clearly audible sound from things above and heavenly. When we hear 'song', we learn in a figure the outward decorum of life. For from musical instruments only the sound of the melody strikes the ears, and the words being sung are not articulated by the notes; but in song both occur together,

both the rhythm of the melody and the force of the words carried along with the melody, a force that must remain unknown when the melody is produced by instruments alone. So too it is with those who pursue virtue. Some, applying their minds to the contemplative and visionary philosophy of what exists, achieve virtue unseen by the many, keeping the good shut up in their own conscience. Others also order the conduct of their life with diligence, and by their outward decorum they publish, as if in words, the good rhythm of their own life. When, therefore, the good is achieved in both ways, moral philosophy joining with contemplative, the result is 'A song of a psalm' or 'A psalm of a song'. But when only one of the two is set forth for praise, either the good of the mind is signified by 'Psalm' alone, or conduct and outward decorum are expressed by 'Song'. A hymn or praise joined with a song becomes a precept that we should not venture upon thoughts about God before we have made our life worthy of such boldness. For 'Praise is not fitting', it says, 'in the mouth of a sinner'; and 'To the sinner God said, Why do you recount my statutes?' In the same way 'A prayer with a song' teaches us the same thing: first to take pains over our life, so that no one is found careless and out of tune in their conduct, and only then to approach God in prayer. It seems to me that the Lord conveyed this very thought to those who said to him, 'Teach us to pray', since prayer is accomplished not in words but in life, when he says, 'If you forgive people their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.' When 'Praise' is written by itself, its meaning contains a testimony about the one who offers the praises to God. For praising God does not belong to just anyone; rather, it says, 'A praise of David', so that we may learn from this that if we become like him, then we too shall receive the boldness to praise God. 'A psalm in hymns' leads us up to a loftier state, one which the divine Apostle also knew, as he tells the Corinthians that he sings now with the spirit and now with the mind. So psalmody joined with the mind interprets what was said before, that the outward must be

worthy of the hidden, so that the song may signify [?] such a thought. But psalmody accomplished by the spirit alone shows the exalted state of the saints, when what is offered [?] to God is better than any display through outward things. For it does not say 'in songs' that articulate the force of thoughts through words, but 'A psalm in hymns'. This, in my judgement, means [?] to know from the hymn. For we learn that [?] a life that sets its mind on things above, and [?] from heavenly and supernal thoughts [?] our instrument: this is a hymn to God, not in the power of words but in a life rightly lived in that exalted state. And when the inscription adds the word 'of understanding' to the hymns, the word seems to me to be giving a kind of counsel [?] to be understanding in what we offer for the glorification of God, so that we do not unwittingly, through some unexamined [?] impulse, ascribe to the divine majesty thoughts that are unfitting. One such thought is supposing that for those who live according to God the rewards are laid up in the prosperity [?] of this life, and thinking that whatever seems good to human perception is also judged good by God. Many such thoughts [?] can be found in the notions about God put forward [?] by the unintelligent. But you need understanding [?] to know what will bring no blame on the one who offers it. For to offer him praise truly worthy of him is beyond what [?] human [?] can find; for us it is enough, not to discover knowledge about him, but [?] not to be carried into anything incongruous. This is what we understood about 'the praise of David': that [?] divine praise is fitting [?]. In the same way, it seems to me, we should understand prayer when we hear 'A prayer of David [?]': that we must strive to make our life like his, so that we may acquire the boldness to pray [?]… 'and pours out his supplication before the Lord' [?]. For we need [?] understanding of God, so that we may perceive in what we are poor; for we would not come to desire the true goods unless we recognized our poverty in such things. But one becomes [?] earnest and wholehearted in prayer when we know in what we are poor and grow weary at the delay of what we long for. And so our supplication is poured out through the eyes, using tears in place of words.

In the same way you will understand 'A prayer of Moses, the man of God': that it is not possible to approach God in prayer in any other way unless one withdraws from this world and becomes the man of God alone.

CHAPTER 4. The inscription 'For those who will be changed' seems to me to have this meaning: the divine nature alone is above turning and change. It has nothing toward which it could turn, since it is wholly incapable of receiving evil and cannot be turned toward the better. There is nothing toward which it could undergo change, for it has nothing better than itself to pass over to. But we human beings are subject to turning and change, and through this capacity for change we become either worse or better in either direction: worse when we drift away from our share in the goods, and better again when we are changed toward the better. Since, then, we were carried into evil by turning, we need a good change, so that through it a transformation toward the better may come about in us. This is clear from the words written together with 'for those who will be changed'. For the word not only advises that we must be changed; it also suggests a way by which this may be achieved, showing in advance, through certain examples, the change toward the better. The wording of the inscription is this: 'For the end, for those who will be changed, for an inscription on a pillar, for David, for teaching, when he burned Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria of Sobal, and Joab returned and struck the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.' It is clear from these words that the passage contains teaching and counsel, since it says, 'For an inscription on a pillar, for David, for teaching'. 'Teaching' would not have been added if the passage were not aimed at instruction. And 'for an inscription on a pillar' shows that we must keep the word in our memory indelible and deeply imprinted, so that the soul's memory is the pillar, and the letters cut into the pillar are the examples of the good. These were the exploits of the commander-in-chief of David's army, by which the enemies suffered a twofold fate: some were consumed by fire, others destroyed by the sword. Syria between the rivers is consumed by fire… [Editor's notes: (57*) the edition reads χρήσηται; (58*) the edition reads δέξηται.]

…[the Valley of Salt is] slaughtered in twelve thousands. But to set out the historical sequence in detail would be long and at the same time superfluous. What more would we gain by learning a sequential account of what happened? Instead, I think it better to set out briefly in this discourse what the figure in the historical record points to, so that this 'inscription on a pillar' may serve us 'for teaching' about our own life. What, then, do I mean? The text calls the whole nation Syria, but divides it into two parts, marking each with its own distinguishing features: one is called Mesopotamia of Syria, and the other is named Syria of Sobal. Both alike are burned. After this, on the commander's return, the Valley of Salt is condemned to death in twelve thousands. Let us understand, then, that Syria is of two kinds. Some of its people are enclosed on every side by the streams between the rivers; these would be those who are flooded on all sides by the passions. Others are devoted to Sobal, the word signifying by this name [?] the tyranny of the opposing power. This, then, would be our path of change toward the better: that this twofold nation of evil be wiped out by the purifying fire. For as virtue is marked by life and by thought, so evil too is seen in these two. The disorder of life, in which the streams of the passions surround the soul, is called 'between the rivers'; while that which, through wicked doctrines, is devoted to the ruler of this world is named Syria of Sobal. When these have been consumed by the burning and purifying word, it then follows that the barren and salty land, which is the camp of the opposing powers, is brought down by the commander-in-chief's blow. For victory over the enemies would not come to us unless the commander of the armies prevailed with his hand. Peace follows naturally upon the destruction of the enemies. This is the consequence of victory, and it is with this in view that the inscription engraves upon our memories the guidance toward being changed, showing through historical examples our deliverance from the passions. The lesson about change would become still clearer to us if we followed the other translators. Instead of 'change', one of them wrote 'For the flowers' and another 'For the lilies'. The flower indicates the change from winter to spring, which signifies the passage from vice to the life of virtue. The sight of the lily explains what the change must lead to: whoever has become bright through change has plainly exchanged a black and darkened form for one that is bright and white as snow… [Editor's notes: (68) σημειούμενος is omitted in the edition; (70) the edition reads κατεμπίμπραται; (71) the edition reads ποταμίοις; (77) the edition reads προσέγραφεν.]

…Wherever, then, 'For those who will be changed' is added to an inscription, I think we must take from the word this counsel: that we must always, through prayer and care for our life, acquire a change toward the better.

CHAPTER 5. The inscription 'For the hidden things' sets before us the attainment of accuracy in the knowledge of God. The worst fall of the soul is a mistaken notion about the Divine; for what would anyone gain from good things if they did not possess the Good itself? For this reason the inscription holds out to you, like a lamp, the word that searches out the hidden things of the knowledge of God, whose chief point is faith in the Son. For that is what the inscription says: 'For the hidden things of the Son'. That which is incomprehensible and invisible and beyond every apprehending thought is truly hidden, and whoever has drawn near to it by faith has reached the very goal of victory. The meaning of 'For her who inherits' is plain. The Prophet brings this intercession to God on behalf of the soul that has fallen from its own inheritance, when the sun set upon the one who had transgressed the commandment. He prays that in the morning it may once more put off the darkness and become worthy of that sweet voice which says to those on the right: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.' Anyone who understands 'For the morning help' in this same sense would not miss what is right. For in the usage of Scripture 'the morning' means the dawn. And dawn is the time on the boundary between night and day, when the one vanishes and the other begins. Since evil is often signified in Scripture under the figure of darkness, when the dawn of the virtuous life rises in us through divine help, then we shall reach victory, 'having put off the works of darkness and walking decently as in the day', as the Apostle says. Close to what we have examined is the meaning of 'the Eighth'. For all the care given to a virtuous life looks to the age to come. The beginning of that age is called the Eighth, because it follows the time of the senses, which revolves in weeks. The inscription 'For the Eighth' therefore counsels us not to look to the present time but to look to the Eighth. For when this flowing and transient time comes to an end, in which one thing comes into being and another is dissolved, and when the need for coming into being has passed and what is dissolved no longer exists, the hoped-for resurrection [will transform] into some other

[?] …a state of life that transforms our nature. And when the transient nature of time comes to an end, and the activity of birth and decay no longer exists, then the week that measures out time will certainly come to a stop as well, and that eighth day will take its place, which is the age to come. That age becomes wholly one single day, as one of the prophets says when he calls the life we hope for “the great day.” For it is not the sun of the senses that lights that day but the true light, the sun of righteousness, whom prophecy names “the Dayspring” because he is never hidden by any setting. We have understood the same thing in the inscriptions “For the winepresses.” A winepress is a workshop for wine: the clusters are crushed in it, and the wine comes out [?]. But if the wine flows from rotten or unripe grapes, it at once turns sour and unfit to drink. It goes off into a foul smell or turns to vinegar, and through some further corruption it changes into a breeding-ground for worms. But if the cluster put into the presses is of good stock and ripe, the wine that flows from the clusters will be sweet and fragrant, and with long keeping it grows in beauty and bouquet. What, then, does the riddle mean? That we should take the greatest possible care of the cluster. Why? So that the storehouse of the human mind may be rich for us. That storehouse is hope, in which all the provision for our life is kept. The nature of the clusters would become plain to us if the branches were made clear first, along with the vine that holds both clusters and branches. This will become clear from the words of the Lord, who said, “I am the vine, you are the branches.” For if we are truly in him, “rooted,” “bearing fruit and growing,” as the Apostle says, then we shall understand from these words that we, who were created in him and have no being without him, are required by him to yield a cluster of works worthy of the sap that nourishes us. It must not be sour and harsh through anger, nor spoiled and dissolved in rottenness through some pleasure. For in the winepress of each person's soul (and the winepress is the conscience), the cluster of our works will become our wine for the life to come. And every one of us must take his fill of his own labours, whatever kind they turn out to be. Blessed indeed are those vinedressers whose wine, when it is enjoyed, “gladdens the heart of man.” But pitiable on the other hand, and worthy of lament, are those whose wine becomes “the rage of dragons,” in the words of Moses, having turned into a poisonous quality

from the vine-shoots of Sodom, to their destruction. So if you look toward the Eighth, the inscription says, remember the winepresses, so that through your good works your presses may overflow with fragrant wine, as the proverb puts it. CHAPTER 6. The inscription “For Maeleth” has been rendered more clearly by those who translated this word into Greek. It puts eagerness into those who contend for virtue by showing what the end of the contests is like: it says that dances and festivities are laid up for those who have won the contests, since the word has been interpreted with this meaning. For “Maeleth” is said to mean “through dances.” We learned something like this from the story of David's victory. When Goliath fell in single combat with the youth, the young women honoured his hard struggle by coming out to meet him with dances. In the same way the inscription about Maeleth says that every victory won against our adversaries by sweat and toil is welcomed with festivity and choral dancing, as the whole intelligible creation joins itself to the victors in the harmony of a chorus. For there was a time when rational nature formed a single chorus. It looked to the one leader of the chorus and wound through the dance in the harmony that he gave to its movement through the commandment. But sin broke in and dissolved that divine concord of the chorus. It poured the slipperiness of deceit beneath the feet of the first human beings, who were dancing together with the angelic powers, and it brought about a fall. Through that fall humanity was torn away from its union with the angels, since the fall dissolved their fellowship [?]. For this reason the one who has fallen needs much sweat and toil.
