He must struggle against the one who presses down on him where he has fallen and throw him off, so that he may stand upright again and receive the divine chorus as the prize of his victory over his opponent in the wrestling. So when you hear the inscription joining “For Maeleth” to the phrase “To the end,” know that through the riddle you are being counselled not to grow slack in the contests of temptation but to look to the end, which is victory. And this means being enrolled in the angelic chorus, with your soul purified by the onslaught of temptations. We have heard from the Lord's own voice that this happened in the case of Lazarus. Through his patient endurance of sufferings he kept himself from falling throughout the whole racecourse of his life. When his

tent was dissolved and the one wrestling against him had been defeated in the stadium of life, he was at once among the angels. For it says, “It came to pass that the poor man died and was carried away by the angels.” This is the dance: the journey with the angels. And the bosom of the patriarch, who takes Lazarus into himself, is not thought of as standing outside the bright harmony of the chorus either. When you hear “bosom,” you would not go wrong in understanding it as a wide expanse like that of the sea: the fullness of good things, for which the patriarch was named, and in which Lazarus too comes to be. For among those who have shone in similar contests, nothing belongs to any one person privately. The good becomes common to all who have run together by the same virtue toward an equal good. The inscription that speaks of “the departure from the tent,” and again the one “For the dedication of the house of David,” stand next to each other in both position and meaning. One is in the twenty-eighth psalm and the other in the one after it. The wording of each is as follows. The first inscription reads, “A psalm of David, of the departure from the tent”; the next reads, “A psalm of the dedication of the house of David.” For unless we go out from the tent of the senses, our true house is not dedicated. What this means is the following. Two kinds of life are recognised in human nature. One is the life of the flesh, which works through the senses. The other is the spiritual and immaterial life, which is achieved by the intellectual and bodiless life of the soul. But it is impossible to share in both at the same time, for devotion to one of them brings about the loss of the other. So if we mean to make the soul a dwelling place of God, we must go out from the tent of the flesh. Our house cannot be dedicated in any other way by the one who renews us by dwelling in us, unless the departure from the tent has been accomplished by our becoming strangers to bodily life. The psalm “of Ecstasy,” placed after the dedication, bears this inscription: “To the end, a psalm of David, of ecstasy.” It agrees with what we have already considered, for it counsels us to stand outside those things whose company does us harm. In the psalms to which “For remembrance” is attached, the word sets before us a brief lesson about our salvation. Disobedience to the divine commandment became for humanity the one road to destruction, for we would not have perished if we had kept the commandment in memory. For

this reason the word sets before us the remembrance of the commandment as an antidote to the disease of forgetfulness, and it does so in two psalms. In the psalms to which “confession” is attached, the word teaches us the following. In the usage of Scripture, confession has two meanings: sometimes it means the declaring of sins, and at other times thanksgiving. Here we are guided toward the virtuous life in both senses. Confessing our sins brings about separation and estrangement from evil. And eagerness to give thanks increases the favour of the Benefactor toward those who receive his kindnesses with a grateful sense of them. So the psalm is set out “For confession” in this way: if some memory of sin smoulders within you, it counsels the cleansing that comes through repentance; but if your life is going well and growing better, it makes your better choice firm through thanksgiving to God. The phrase “Inscription on a pillar” and the phrase “Destroy not” are found in some of the inscriptions, sometimes together and sometimes separately. They contain counsel about the virtue of long-suffering. “Destroy not” are the words of David when he stopped his armour-bearer from striking Saul. The meaning of “Inscription on a pillar” is that we must have such a saying engraved on the memory of the soul as on a pillar. Then in similar situations, if some circumstance stirs up our anger to take revenge on the one who has hurt us, we may read in our mind the command that forbids killing, and we ourselves may lull our anger into long-suffering. But we shall discuss these matters more precisely later, when we return to the study of the remaining inscriptions.

CHAPTER 7. We must also consider what “Alleluia” means, since it serves as the inscription of many psalms. “Alleluia,” then, is a mystical exhortation that rouses the ear to hymn God, so that its meaning is “Praise the Lord.” For in those parts of holy Scripture where this word is attached, saying

[?] …of the names for God among the Hebrews, he says, is also “Ia,” while “Allelu” is understood to mean praise. Do not be surprised if this form of the word indicates what is called the nominative case of the noun. The words of the Hebrews are not shaped according to our usage; they pronounce names after a different pattern from ours. For example, when we put the prophet's name into Greek according to our own pattern, we say “Elias,” but in the Hebrew idiom the nominative of the name is “Eliu.” It is the same here: when the Hebrew tongue wants to signify praise in the nominative case, it calls it “Allelu.” And since praise is in every case directed to God, and “Ia” is one of the names that express the divine nature, the whole word “Alleluia” taken together is translated “praise of God.” So whenever this word is written at the head of a psalm, it must be understood that what follows is to be referred entirely to the glorification of God. That is why most inscriptions of this kind are found above all in the last parts of the book of Psalms. From this we can understand that praising God is fitting for those who have already reached the perfection of the virtuous life and have been purified by the earlier sections of the psalter, according to the contemplation we found in them. It is fitting for them to be in the state in which the nature of the angels is believed to be. For we have learned of no other occupation of the angels except praising God, and those who are perfect in virtue strive for nothing else than to make their life a praise of God. Since, then, nearly all the psalms with the inscription “Alleluia” are found in the last section of the psalter, it is clear that this last section, which consists mostly of the praise of God or of exhortation to praise God, stands above the whole lofty ascent made through the psalms.

CHAPTER 8. It remains to understand, as far as we can, the reason for the psalms without inscriptions. Let what we have found on this point be submitted to the judgment of our readers. They may accept our views, or lead their minds on to a higher contemplation. We have noticed the following difference among the psalms without inscriptions. In some of them the meaning of the psalm itself takes the place of an inscription. For these, the Hebrews and we agree that the contents have no inscription other than the meaning that appears in the words. The rest do have inscriptions, which are ecclesiastical and mystical and point to the piety of our mystery. But the Hebrews do not have these inscriptions,

in keeping with the charge brought against them in the Gospel, “that they had decreed that if anyone confessed Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue.” So whatever inscriptions they perceived to contain some hint of the mystery, they did not accept. That is why the text has carefully noted this about them, adding to the reading of the ecclesiastical inscription that “among the Hebrews it is without inscription.” Now that this distinction among the uninscribed psalms has been set out, it is time to confirm the argument from the words of the psalms themselves. The psalm placed first of all needed no inscription. Its aim is plain to readers: it is an introduction to the life of wisdom. It counsels us to turn away from evil, to dwell in the good, and to become like God as far as we are able. But since the first beatitude begins with the warning against impiety, the second psalm proposes how we may come to be free of impiety, and it proclaims the mystery of the gospel in advance. In a way, then, the first psalm is the inscription of the second. For the second psalm speaks of the birth in the flesh of him who was begotten “today” for our sake (“today” is a part of time), and who is always the Son and God, from the Father and in the Father. It also speaks of his kingship over those who had no king. Because they did not serve God, these were counted among the nations. They governed themselves, or rather they were lawless, since they did not accept the divine law but threw off its yoke from themselves; and by “yoke” the psalm means the commandment. But when the kingdom that rules over all came to them too, those who once had no master became God's inheritance through faith in the one begotten today, that is, the one established as king over them. And they themselves were also begotten and became kings. Over them the iron rod, that is, the unchangeable power, shattered what was earthly and made of clay and changed them into incorruptible nature. It taught that the only blessed thing is to trust in him. Such is the meaning of the psalm, as I have explained it. Anyone who wishes may test our view against the divine words themselves, to see whether what we have said fits the divinely inspired Scripture. The other uninscribed psalms are of the second kind described above: they lack inscriptions in the synagogue of the Hebrews, not in the Church of God. For in every one of them one can certainly find some inscription

that the Hebrew does not accept because of the message of true religion, and that they refused through unbelief. To put it summarily, there are twelve such psalms. To set them out more precisely and give the order in which each comes, they are: the thirty-second and the forty-second; after these the seventieth, then the third after it; and after these the ninetieth. Then the ninety-second and the following ones up to the ninety-sixth; then the ninety-eighth; and, last among the uninscribed, the hundred and third. This, then, is the list of the psalms that have no inscription among the Hebrews. I think the reason they did not accept these inscriptions is none other than the one already given. Our argument would be better proved if we looked briefly and quickly at some of the uninscribed psalms, so that the charge against the Jews' ingratitude may be confirmed by studying the words themselves. The psalm commands us to rejoice in the one who came from heaven to earth, saying, “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous.” He is the one who presides over all, who brought the universe from nothing into being and keeps all things in being, whose command becomes substance. This is the meaning of the divine words: “He spoke, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created.” He makes blessed the nation that rests on his name. By “the nation” the psalm means us, whose hope of salvation is the name of Christ, after whom we believers are named. “For the Lord looked down from heaven to see all the sons of men, from his prepared dwelling place.” By “his prepared dwelling place” the psalm means the Father, who always is: his being is eternal, not having come from anything, but always ready. We are not surprised that from that dwelling place he mingles with the sons of men by becoming Son of Man, because we are convinced that he is “the one who fashioned our hearts one by one.” For if human nature is his handiwork, what new thing do we learn from the mystery? That the Master of nature came to his own, but the Hebrews did not receive him. That is why they have no inscription, just as there is no sun for someone who cannot see. So we judge that the fleshly course of the law, which the psalm calls a “false horse,” is useless for salvation. So is every bodily understanding of the commandments, and this would be the giant. The Psalmist disparages such things in a riddle, saying:

“The horse is a false hope for salvation, and a giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength.” But we look to the one who rescues our souls from death through heavenly food. As the Prophet says, “The eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, on those who hope in his mercy, to rescue their souls from death and to keep them alive in famine.” So we say, “Our soul will wait for the Lord,” who looked upon us from heaven. And again, “Let your mercy, Lord, be upon us, as we have hoped in you.”

For these reasons the Hebrew does not accept the inscription of this psalm. In the same way, the forty-second psalm has no inscription among the Hebrews. I think the text shows that the mystery in this psalm could not be accepted by those who follow the Hebrew party. For the psalmist promises to go in to the altar, having been made young again. But this does not belong to the Hebrew, for he will not consent to be renewed by the mystery of salvation through being born from above. In the seventieth psalm the ecclesiastical edition has the inscription “For the sons of Jonadab and the first who were taken captive,” but among the Hebrews this has been passed over in silence. The reason is clear. The prophecy about the Lord is more plainly visible here, and so the unbelief of the Jews is exposed, since they were unable to accept the clear teaching of the mystery. Think of people with diseased eyes and people who have fallen ill with hydrophobia. The first cannot bear the stroke of the sun's rays, and the second cannot bear the sight of water. They shut their eyelids: those with sore eyes to shield themselves from the rays, and those who dread water to shield themselves from the sight of it. In the same way, the wickedness of the Jews will not confess the glory of the divine proclamation, and so by keeping silent it makes the truth something they cannot accept. One can also recognise the riddles of the prophecy from the psalm itself. For it says in the seventieth psalm, whose inscription is “Concerning the first who were taken captive,” as if from the person [?]

…me, and from the depths of the earth you brought me up again; you increased your greatness upon me, and you turned and comforted me.” We will understand this more clearly from the teaching of the great Paul: how someone dragged down into the abyss by the weight of sin is brought up from the depths through the one who went down into the abyss for our sake. About him Paul says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’ (that is, to bring Christ down), or ‘Who will go down into the abyss?’ (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).” Death was driven out by the same way it entered the world. It entered through a man, and through a man it is expelled. The first man opened the way in for death; through the second, life is brought in to take its place, and life's entry brings about the disappearance of death. For this reason, since death held the captive in the abyss of death, he went down into this abyss through his passion in order to gather [the captive] to himself again and bring [?] up to the things above. The great voice of the Apostle made these things precisely clear. Among many other things he said about them, he also said this: “As in Adam we all die, so in Christ we shall all be made alive.” This is why the Hebrews stop their ears and do not accept the inscription “For the first captives,” since it proclaims that the Lord's dispensation through the flesh took place for them. In the same way, in the ninetieth psalm you will find the same reason for the Hebrews' refusal to accept the inscription, which reveals the divine manifestation of Christ. For us the psalm just mentioned is “A Praise [?],” and praise is directed to God. But the Hebrews silence the praise and order those who praise the Lord to be silent. At any rate, in the temple they try to stop the children from praising the Lord for his good works, as the Gospel publicly exposes their ingratitude. It would be superfluous to show through contemplation that the words of praise in this song look to the Lord, because the plain wording of the text displays this meaning quite openly. Again, the psalm after the ninety-first has something even more evident in its inscription, and that is why the Judaizer refuses to assent to it. Its wording is: “A praise of a song of David, for the day of the Sabbath, when the earth was settled.” Who among those who have received the teaching of true religion does not know that the mystery concerning death was accomplished on the day of the Sabbath, when that body of the Lord's lay [?] motionless in the tomb as in a bed? And on that day, when the earth was settled by our founder, who… [Apparatus: “shall be made alive,” ed.; “first” omitted in ed.; “accept,” ed.]

…by destroying the destroyer of our dwelling, built again from the beginning what had fallen into ruin? Our destroyer was death. He abolished death at the very time when he seemed to us to be keeping Sabbath, lying motionless in the place where he was. All the while he was overcoming the power of death and opening through himself, for all the dead, the way to resurrection from death. But the enemy of the cross of Christ does not accept the mystery of the Sabbath. That is why this praise too is uninscribed among them. He does not agree that this is the Lord who shaped himself to our likeness and wrapped himself in our shame in the form of a slave, and then reigned again, put on his own majesty and girded himself with his own power. The power and majesty of the Son is the Father. Human nature had been loosened by sin, and he made it firm again, so that it can no longer be pushed toward evil or be tossed about by sin. After celebrating this grace in many other riddles, the psalmist adds to his words certain rivers that roar loudly, by which I think he means the voices of the Gospels. Why go through every detail written in the song of the psalm? The divine words leave no doubt that the hymn looks to him, the God who went up with a shout, whose testimonies were confirmed through the good confession, and who prepared the holiness of the Spirit to adorn his own house, the Church. For the same reason the Hebrew does not accept the inscription of the third psalm after the ninetieth either. Its wording is: “For David, on the fourth day of the week; uninscribed among…”

The mystery in this foretells the dispensation of the passion. On the fifth day of the week (Judas's betrayal having taken place on the day before), the one who redeems the whole world through himself is, in a way, sold by the traitor. This is the name Jeremiah's prophecy gives to the event: “And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who was priced.” I think he is sold so that by his own sale he might buy back those who had been sold under sin. So the Prophet, foreseeing what would happen, is stirred by something like anger at what was done, and calls upon the God of vengeance [?]…

…divinity. As he says elsewhere, it is characteristic of the fool to say that the God who is does not exist. To such people he says: “Understand, you fools among the people; you simpletons, at last be wise. Who planted the ear? Who formed the eye? Who instructs the nations? Who knows people's thoughts?” I think that through all these words the Prophet points to the miracles of healing. Eyes were formed with spittle and earth worked into clay, and hearing was, in a way, planted by his fingers in those who lacked this sense. Whatever lay hidden in the secret places of people's minds was exposed by the one who sees their inner thoughts. Since he was not heard when he cried these things out to them, he turns his words to the Lord and says: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach out of your law.” He speaks as though the law by itself is no help unless some divine teaching makes clear the mystery it contains. As this same prophet said: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive the wonders of your law.” Or perhaps he calls blessed the person from the Gentiles who believes in the spiritual law. Such a person was a mere man before this time, fleshly and compared to the beasts, but becomes blessed in the instruction of the divine law, once the curse has been turned into blessing. For him wrath is softened and he is spared the evil days, while for the other a pit is dug. Then, a little further on, the psalmist states the purpose of the Lord's dispensation as a man: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would soon have dwelt in Hades.” The Lord's help did not let us become sojourners in Hades. He also teaches that the healing we received from the healer was a counterweight matching the multitude of our pains from sin. … And he expounds a greater truth still, laying down that evil does not exist from eternity. He says: “The throne of lawlessness, which fashions trouble by decree, shall have no part with you.” This means: the beginning of evil is not seen together with you. The throne stands for the beginning, which creates sin by decree. By these words he showed that evil neither exists from eternity nor will remain for ever. What did not always exist will not exist for ever either. He also describes how evil is to be done away with, foretelling the disappearance of evil in the bloodguilt the Jews incurred against the Lord. He says: “They hunt after the soul of the righteous, and they will condemn innocent blood.” But this becomes salvation for me. Through this, the Lord who was condemned to death becomes my refuge. This God becomes a help and a hope for those who have believed. In just judgment he renders to each what they deserve, and he will destroy the wickedness of sinners, not their nature. So he says in these words: “And he will repay [?]…” [Apparatus: “but to that one,” etc.]

“…the Lord will repay them for their lawlessness, and according to their wickedness the Lord God will destroy them.” By these words he signifies that those who are now shaped by sin will be destroyed. When evil no longer exists, neither will anyone shaped by it. So when evil has perished and no trace of that character remains in anyone, all will be shaped after Christ, and one form will shine out in everyone: the form impressed on our nature from the beginning.

CHAPTER 9. After this he proceeds in order. He uses no musical instrument, but offers God the joyful praise in song with his own voice. He says: “A praise of a song for David.” This inscription too is absent among the Hebrews. The psalm calls its hearers to share in exultation and to raise a shout of victory, saying: “Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us shout to God our Saviour.” Toward the end it contains a rather vehement threat against the unbelievers. They showed the same ill will during the forty years spent in the desert, when they provoked their benefactor, and afterwards when they refused the rest from sin given to us through the Gospel. They could have heard “today” the voice of the one who for our sake entered into the “today,” coming down from his eternal majesty, which is before the ages, into birth in time, and so opened for themselves the entrance into rest. But they always took error and unbelief as their guides, in earlier times and later ones alike, and so they were shut out by an oath from entering God's rest. How could they enter the rest when they had willingly made themselves strangers to the blessing? In the same way, the ninety-fifth psalm, which follows these, is said by those who follow the Hebrew text to be uninscribed. For us, however, it is a song sung to God after the return from captivity, when the structure of our nature, which had been dissolved, was rebuilt. This is the wording of the inscription: “A praise of a song, when the house was built after the captivity; uninscribed among the Hebrews.” At its very opening the psalm proclaims the good news of the mystery of the New Covenant, saying: “Sing to the Lord a new song.” It is fitting that the Hebrews have suppressed the inscription of this psalm, because after the radiant gospel proclamations at its opening, the prophecy addresses its words to those from the Gentiles, saying:

“Bring to the Lord, you families of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honour, and worship the Lord in his holy court; take up sacrifices and enter his courts.” The whole passage that follows is of the same kind, foretelling that the blessing will pass over to the nations. It says: “Say among the nations, ‘The Lord has reigned’”; and he set right the world that evil had loosened, so that it stays unshaken for ever. At this “the heavens are glad and all the earth exults, while the waters of the sea are shaken with all that fills them.” By these words he points figuratively to the opposing power, which is troubled and thrown off balance by our life when we become heavens declaring the glory of God, or earth blessed by bearing the fruit of the virtues. For it says: “Let the sea be shaken, and all that fills it.” He says the plains will rejoice, and by “plains” he means a life that is level in virtue. Isaiah mentions this too in his own words, in another way, when he commands the ravines to be filled and the hills and mountains to be brought low. It seems to me he means nothing other than that he wants to cure the deficiencies and excesses in the practice of virtue, so that the standard of virtue is neither hollowed out by a lack of good nor made uneven by excess. It says: “The plains will rejoice, and all that is in them.” In the same way, the Hebrews did not accept the inscription of the next psalm, because it speaks of our affairs and proclaims the good news of how our land was established. The inscription ascribes the psalm to David and reads: “For David, when his land was established.” Clearly “his” refers not to David but to God. The land that earlier fell away through evil has now gained stability through the knowledge of God. We are all God's land. Earlier we wavered in the good and so came under the curse, but afterwards we were rescued from the curse and once again found stability in the good. The opening of the psalm proclaims this good news at once: when the Lord has become king, the earth rejoices. It is as if someone said that when the sun shines, the earth is lit up. In the same way, when the Lord's kingdom prevails, the joy of the kingdom is within us. The wording is: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth exult; let the many islands be glad.” He rightly calls “islands” the souls of those who stay steadfast and immovable in temptations. The brine of evil surrounds them on every side, but when it beats against them it is not strong enough to make the firmness of virtue waver. Then, between these, the incomprehensibility of the divine…

[?] … in the cloud and the darkness he signifies the [?] in a riddle. For it says: “Cloud [and darkness are] round about him.” Having pointed to [?], by which it says that “fire will go before him and blaze round about his enemies,” he reveals [?], meaning by the lightnings the words of the divine preaching, which [shone out] over the whole world. For it says: “His lightnings shone out on the world.” And he pointed to the [?] of the Gospel mysteries for the [?] when he said: “The heavens proclaimed his righteousness, and all the peoples saw his glory.” He [foretells] the overthrow of idols and the disappearance of that error when he says: “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame”; in this way he brings about the dissolution of what was badly put together. [?] … he brings into upheaval not what is heavenly in us but what is earthly, saying in these words: “He who sits upon the cherubim: let the earth be shaken.” I pass over what follows so as not to burden the course of the interpretation with a great crowd of material. I say only this: everything looks to one and the same goal right to the end of the psalm. He testifies that this God who has become king has not appeared to us now for the first time, but was also manifest to the famous prophets. So he mentions Moses, Aaron and Samuel, each of whom is renowned and celebrated for his devotion to God. He also adds the pillar of cloud, in which God spoke with them. By this, I think, he teaches the unbelievers not to be surprised at the [?] of the [?] that came about through a man… [Apparatus: “exalts,” ed.]

…[of the one] who perceived [him] through the cloud. For it says: “Behold, the Lord sits on a light cloud.” The same prophet also calls those who follow him “clouds,” where he says: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” By giving them the same name, clouds, he shows the kinship between the Lord's flesh and the rest of human nature. So David, going on, says to this God, who once spoke to people through a cloud and afterwards through flesh: “O Lord our God, you heard them; O God, you were gracious to them, while taking vengeance on all their deeds.” Someone looking at the dispensation might slip into lowly, human notions about the Divine. To prevent this, he adds these words at the end of the psalm, turning to us: “Exalt the Lord our God, and worship at the footstool of his feet, for he is holy.” We take the meaning of these words to be this: “People, the divine mysteries have been made known to you as far as human hearing can receive them. Let them guide you to a reverent knowledge of God, and exalt God's glory as far as your reason can reach. But know this: however far your understanding stretches, and however far it passes beyond every lofty imagining in its thoughts about God, what you find and worship is not the very majesty of the one you seek, but the footstool of his feet.” By this phrase he means what lies beneath and below our understanding, compared with an apprehension that cannot be attained. After this, passing over quite a few psalms in between, in the hundred and third, which it showed to be the last of the many uninscribed among the Hebrews, he speaks plainly of the Only-begotten as God and ascribes to him the cause of the founding of the universe. The inscription says that this psalm, which is David's and concerns the creation of the world, is uninscribed among the Hebrews. This indicates that they do not accept the purpose of this prophecy. The inscription reads: “Of David, on the creation of the world; uninscribed among the Hebrews.” We will set out the meaning of this psalm in due course. For now it is enough to say that the same cause, I mean the unbelief of the Jews, made the inscription of this psalm too unacceptable to the Hebrews.

CHAPTER 10. Nor should we pass over the diapsalma without considering it. Those before us held that the diapsalma signifies a change of thought, of speaker or of subject. We do not reject the views of the Fathers, but we will not hesitate to contribute some thoughts of our own on the meaning of this term. Here is the meaning we have found for the diapsalma: as the psalm proceeds in order, which

…came about [?] of David, again another [?] and some addition to the gift of knowledge, for the benefit of those receiving the prophecy. He held back his [voice?], giving his mind time to receive the [?] of what was happening in him through the divine illumination. Think of people travelling together on a road, or talking with one another at banquets or gatherings. If a sudden sound reaches them from somewhere, they often stop speaking and turn their minds intently toward it, quietly giving their hearing time to grasp what the sound means; then, when the sound has stopped, they take up their conversation again. In the same way the great [David], prophesying by the Spirit, [?] what he had already learned [?] in the melody. And if, while he was speaking, he [perceived] something, he lent his soul's hearing to the one who was [?] spiritually and hushed the song. Then, once he was full of the thoughts, he went through them again, weaving the words into the melody. So the diapsalma, if one were to put it in a definition, is a sudden pause that occurs in the middle of the psalmody so that a thought imparted by God can be received. Or one might better define it as teaching from the Spirit that arises in the soul in an ineffable way, when attention to this thought interrupts the continuous flow of the melody. Many might think the silence meant that the power of the Holy Spirit had left the one prophesying. To prevent this, some of the translators write “Always” at these pauses instead of “diapsalma.” This teaches us that the teaching of the Holy Spirit was always present in the soul, but the word that put into speech the thoughts arising in the soul from God was not always present: at one time it spoke out from the mind, at another it listened and received. While he was declaring the thoughts impressed on his mind, the psalm went on in order; but if something more divine sounded in the hearing of his soul, he gave himself wholly to listening and hushed the song. So, since the Holy Spirit was always speaking in him even during the time of silence, the word came with pauses (and the translators named the pause “diapsalma”). We have observed that the whole Book of Psalms is divided into five parts. From this too it can be shown that the explanation we have arrived at is true: by a kind of steady progress, the one guided through the book is always led by the hand to something higher through each of its sections. Only the last section has, in each of its psalms, a continuous and unbroken hymn from beginning to end, nowhere divided by a diapsalma. This holds both for the song in each of the Ascents and for the psalms whose inscription is “Alleluia.” I think this observation shows that in the other sections, since they are lower, there is room for the

…teaching the higher ideas in addition, and weaving in, along the course of the discourse, things that can lead the mind up toward what is better. But the perfection reached through the "Ascents," and in the psalms headed "Alleluia," needs nothing added, because it has taken hold of the highest of all that can be conceived in relation to the good. It is complete in itself, through every kind of perfection in the good. The meaning of the inscription on these psalms bears witness to this as well, for it names the supreme state simply "praise of God." Bodies grow upward through the stages of life until they reach the point where nature becomes stable. After that they take on nothing more, but remain as they are for all the time that is left. In the same way, divine teaching both grows and comes to rest. Through it Scripture nurses those who are childish and immature in mind with suitable food, with milk and the like, and so leads them to growth. To those who are already mature it sets out the table of solid food, since their soul's senses have been trained beforehand through the other lessons. So the fact that in the last section the prophet of the Spirit nowhere needed to be taught any of the higher things in a diapsalma would be clear proof of what we have said. The point can be understood by setting beside it the parts of the psalmody that are divided by the diapsalma. In the third psalm he first speaks of the distress and helplessness that came upon him when his enemies rose up against him. Then he divides off a section with the diapsalma and takes courage from the saving voice that sounded within him in secret: "But you, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head." Again he makes a pause in the melody, after the thankful words he spoke: "With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain." Then he is taught how the helplessness common to all human ills is resolved. Having been taught the mystery of the Lord's passion in the sudden illumination of the Spirit, he takes on the very person of the Master and says: "I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord will help me." To set out precisely the meaning in each of these words would be superfluous, since the discourse is hurrying on to other things. We must confirm the explanation given of the diapsalma by building the argument from the Scriptures themselves, and at the diapsalma in the fourth psalm we learn the same thing. There he cries out, in a way, to all human nature about the vanity of the things people strive for. He calls the sons of men heavy-hearted, because they love what is vain and the lie that has no substance. Then, after pausing again, he shows where the truth lies: "Know," he says, "that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful." By "holy one" he points, I think, to the Lord, as Moses says: "For the Lord is just and holy."

Next he gives counsel on how one may pass through life in purity. He becomes judge and examiner of the soul's thoughts when he says, "What you say in your hearts, repent of on your beds." Withdrawing into himself again, he both heard of the abolition of the Law's animal sacrifices and proclaims it aloud to his hearers. For he says that whoever needs cleansing of the soul should not rest his hopes on the slaughter of irrational animals, but should recognize the sacrifices that please God. That is why he says: "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord." In the same way, in the seventh psalm the words of petition come first. In them he pleads his case before the just judge: the wickedness of his enemies does not come as retaliation, for they are the ones who began the evil. He holds that it is equally sinful to start wickedness and to repay the one who started it in kind. Having said this, he again lends his ear to the one who reveals the great mystery of godliness, through which the Lord takes vengeance on our true enemies. For the band of our adversaries [?] cannot be overthrown unless the Lord rises up on our behalf, and death must in any case come before resurrection. So he who announced the Lord's resurrection also made known what is bound up with the resurrection, I mean the mystery of the passion. For this reason, filled with God by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, he says: "Arise, O Lord, in your anger; be exalted at the ends of your enemies." By "anger" he signifies the retributive power of the just judge, and by the words that follow, the obliteration of wickedness. For by nature the only enemy is what is seen as the opposite of the good, that is, wickedness. Its end is obliteration and passing over into non-being. So when he says, "Be exalted at the ends of your enemies," he foretells that once the wickedness of the enemies has been brought to its end, no road toward wickedness will be left in life any longer. Health is the end of sickness, and waking the end of sleep. The sleeper does not reach the end of sleep while he is still asleep, and the sick person does not come to the end of illness through the illness itself. But when health has taken the place of sickness in the one, and waking has taken the place of sleep in the other, we say that each has come to the end of the state he was in, the one of sleep and the other of sickness. So here too he called the change of human nature into blessedness "the end of the enemies." In the whole book of Psalms we have noticed only one altered form of the diapsalma, in the ninth psalm. There it says not simply "Diapsalma" but "Song of diapsalma." Perhaps the phrase has been inverted by a copyist's error, so that it ought rather to read "Diapsalma of song" and not "Song of diapsalma." Nevertheless, since we should keep before our eyes what is in

[?] …, we will keep to the sequence handed down to us in this part of Scripture and try to search out the reason for the "song of diapsalma," and what it is. Our view, then, is that from this point up to the next diapsalma there was a single diapsalma, while the Holy Spirit was placing the ideas of the prophecy in David. But it did not happen here as in the other cases,

[?] In the other cases, the instruction that the Spirit gave to the soul in secret and the declaring aloud of the knowledge placed in him did not take place at the same time. While the heart was being taught within, speech fell silent. Here, however, both happened together and at the same moment. The teaching of the higher ideas came to him from the Spirit in the very midst of his prophesying, and the flow of the melody was not broken off. The Holy Spirit, having taken root in the prophet's instrument, moved the organs of speech by its own will, so that the song did not stop and the teaching was not hindered by the sound. For this teaching of the Spirit was itself the melody, as Symmachus calls it. Since a break of this kind occurs in many parts of the psalmody, it should be enough to have offered, in what has been said, a common approach to understanding the diapsalma, without going through every diapsalma in detail. It would be both pointless and superfluous to linger over what is already known and lengthen the [discourse] by repeating what is agreed. [?] CHAPTER 11. [?] …is the Holy Spirit, as [the Lord] says: "He will teach you all things." To this guide and teacher of our souls, all other things seem secondary. His earnest concern is to rescue those who wander in the vanity of life and draw them toward the true life. Everything accomplished with a particular aim in view involves a certain natural and necessary order, which achieves the desired result step by step. Take stone carvers: the aim of their work is to make the stone resemble something that exists. Yet the work does not begin straight away from the finished result. The craft imposes a necessary order on the task, without which the goal could not be achieved. First the stone must be broken away from the rock it grows from, then the useless projections must be cut off, toward the [?]…

[?] For if any one of these is lacking, the name of Christ does not exist. So when this name is exalted in our quiver, that is, when it comes to be in our soul through faith (for the soul is the quiver of the word), it becomes the destroyer of the one who rises up against us and pursues us, whose destruction took place on the wood. That is why the beginning of victory comes after one flees in good time from the one who rises up against us (who is one by nature but becomes a multitude through his evil alliance) and says, "How many are those who afflict me, and many rise up against me," and whatever else the psalmody goes on to contain. For a timely flight from those who rise up against us is the cause of victory over our enemies. That is why the next psalm bears the inscription "To the end." The end of every contest is victory, as our discussion has already explained in detail, and once you have tasted victory, one victory after another is won against the enemies. In the first victory, when the pleasures of life were contending against the goods of the soul, your inclination toward what is better prevailed over material deception. For you condemned those who seek vanity and love the lie, and in place of attachment to visible things you [chose] the [?] of things invisible. In the next psalm you win in another way. Two parties are fighting each other over the inheritance of truth, one putting forward the Law and the other faith, and the just judge of the contest awards you the prize against your opponent. So the pure state of your soul becomes a sunrise for you, since you have left the darkness behind and are bringing on the dawn, which the psalmody calls "morning." So one can see the athlete gaining victory upon victory, the achievements won by victory always advancing toward something greater and more glorious. Then another victory follows in sequence, won by means of what has already been shown. For he who has come to know the inheritance also mentions "the Eighth," which is both the end of the present time and the beginning of the age to come. It is characteristic of "the Eighth" that it no longer gives those who are in it time to prepare good or evil. Instead, it repays with sheaves whatever seeds one has sown for oneself through one's works. That is why he commands that repentance be practiced here, since in Hades such effort accomplishes nothing, [?] once you have been trained by these very victories. Again the word anoints you, like an athlete, for other contests; again it anoints you against the onslaught of temptations. For that same enemy, Absalom, as though born again from us, arms against us that very war that comes from ourselves. But our good counsel in the matter, or rather God's alliance, turns him back as he seeks our death. For since his successes came about through the words of Hushai, he credits them to God, and so

has given his thanksgiving to God. It would be superfluous to set out the history for you in detail: how this Hushai, though loyal to David as one of his shield-bearers, mingled with Absalom's friends and proved more persuasive to the tyrant than Ahithophel's counsel. As a result, when Hushai's proposal won out, the man who had counseled Absalom against David strangled himself. But it would be worthwhile to apply the riddles of the history to the life of virtue as well: how the counsel that saves us becomes a noose for the adversary. This saving counsel is written partly in the history and partly in the psalmody. Our aim, however, is to understand the sequence in the order of the psalms, by which we are brought to the good. So let us consider the counsel here that destroys the one who plots against us. What is it? To consider it equally wicked to begin an injustice and to take revenge on the one who began it. For he calls down the utmost [?] upon himself and sets the punishment against himself, if he should be found to have traded evil for evil as in a business deal, giving back to those who had dealt it out what he had received. And so, after these contests, he is again shown to be the victor. For the inscription "For the winepresses" follows, announcing in advance "the end," and the end of contests is victory. It would be superfluous to unfold again the meaning of "For the winepresses," since it was sufficiently explained when we examined it in its proper place. After the first flight from Absalom he was granted victory by distinguishing vain pursuits from true realities. In the same way now, after similar contests, he uses the word "For the winepresses" as an ally against the adversary and becomes the victor by destroying the enemy and avenger. He is called both enemy and avenger because his very baits to sin are the bitterest punishment for those who perceive them. The means by which he deceitfully draws a person into partnership in evil is itself the most grievous kind of punishment. The divine Apostle interprets this meaning when he says, "receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error." What other device of punishment could be more grievous than the impurity of shameful conduct, which those who practice shameful things work out in themselves? So whoever has destroyed in his own life the power of such a one, who punishes the person living in wickedness through the very fact of sharing in wickedness, sees human beings, and the magnificence enthroned above the heavens, and the dignity of our nature: what it rules over and with whom it is ranked. By the same faculty it governs the irrational creatures and, when compared with the angels, is made only a little lower. It is reason, then, through which we come to rule over the one and gain kinship with the other. Then another kind of victory follows, when one passes beyond

the things that appear and enters into the hidden things by [?] the word, even if you have already been sufficiently trained by the earlier victories. Then you sing "For the secrets of the Son" through a contemplation that is harmonious and in tune. And when you have again overcome the beast that lies in wait against us in hidden places, so that the enemy has no boast left against us ("so that man on earth may no longer boast"), then, through the victory that follows for you in sequence, your trust in God becomes more perfect, and you say: "In the Lord I have put my trust." In the next victory you will again remember "the Eighth," in which "the boastful tongue and the deceitful lips" are destroyed, and the madness against God as well. But those who do not walk around in the circle of ungodliness will be kept from this generation and forever. They hold to the straight way, the new and living way that God has opened for us. But why go through each point one by one? The order and the inscriptions of the psalms sufficiently show you, by this method, the progress toward better things, and the interpretation of the inscriptions offered in the earlier discussions contributes not a little to understanding it.

CHAPTER 12. When the first section of the ascent through the psalms has been completed, the beatitude is repeated in the fortieth psalm, but here the text defines blessedness for us differently than at the beginning. In the first psalm, blessedness lay in turning away from evil. Here, coming to know the good is called blessed. The nature of the good, or whatever word or thought can be found that is higher still, is the only-begotten God, who for our sake became poor though he was rich. Does the text here not foretell the poverty in the flesh that the Gospel narrative has shown us, when it calls blessed the one who has understood that poverty with insight? He is poor in the form of a servant, but blessed in the nature of the Godhead. For after calling him needy and poor at the beginning of the psalm, the text says at the end of the section: "Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. So be it, so be it." Whoever has reached this height begins another ascent. He leaves behind his father Korah, who rose up against the priesthood out of arrogance and for that reason was burned by fire and buried in the chasm, sent under the earth because of his sin. Through faith he makes himself the adopted son of the true Father, understanding how great the difference is between becoming a child of God and being called a son of the rebel Korah. So, having reached the goal of victory and knowing how great the difference is between this Father and the evil father, he devoured and consumed within himself every bestial and venomous thought, according to the

…imitates the nature of deer, which have an inborn power to destroy serpents. It also imitates the deer in its thirst, and it thirsts for the divine springs, which would be the divine nature, one and yet seen in a Trinity. "As the deer," it says, "longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God." Then it comforts the thirst that is gripped by desire. The soul hurries to obtain what it longs for and counts even a short delay in sharing those good things as a misfortune, so both in the middle and at the end of the psalm it says, "Why are you so sorrowful, my soul?" and "Hope in God," since the divine hope truly guarantees us the enjoyment of good things. In this way it goes on to the next psalm, where it is made new through the divine altar. In the one after that it makes victors of those descended from Korah, which shows that a low-born ancestry does not dim a person's standing with God. In this psalm it gives God the credit for overthrowing the enemies when it says, "For you saved us from those who afflict us, and you put to shame those who hate us." Then it passes on to the song of the beloved. So those who were once descended from the apostate and then became victors over the evil one may reach the goal of victory through understanding. For it is "For the end, for understanding, a song for the beloved." There we are taught who it is whose throne has ruled over all things from eternity, and who the virgin is who is brought to him as a bride to share his life. She is counted worthy of this honour only if she forgets her father. After dedicating this song to the beloved, it again presents a victory song for the sons of Korah and leads the discourse through more secret matters, for the psalm's heading reads "concerning the hidden things." There it speaks of "the roar of waters," "the stirring of nations," "the bending of kings," and "the shaking of the earth," and says that "the Lord of all power is with us." Through all of these it foretells the Lord's appearing in the flesh. Nature roars, and the mountains are moved. These mountains are the earthly mindsets of evil, which people of old thought were immovable and unchangeable. The river of gladness gladdens the city of God, and the Most High sanctifies his tabernacle. These and the other things that follow are the riddles through which the word foretells the hidden things. Then the word moves on to another victory: all the nations clap their hands and rejoice, because "God has gone up with a shout." Paul's interpretation gives you a firm account of this going up, for he says that one cannot ascend unless one has first descended. After commanding everyone to sing with understanding, the psalmist moves on to a higher condition and makes "the second day of the week" the subject of his song. Viewed in terms of the first creation, this day saw the making of heaven

and the firmament, and the separation of the waters above heaven from the waters on earth. But if you look to the Gospel, this is truly the day that built heaven for us. God calls the firmament heaven, and Paul understands faith in Christ as the firmament. Heaven is truly created for us by faith at the moment when the gloom of the Sabbath has passed, and we have come to believe the mystery of the Son of God, declared in power according to the spirit of holiness by resurrection from the dead: Jesus our Lord, who is in truth the great Lord, greatly to be praised. Then there is everything the psalm contains next about that divine city, which it also calls "a well-rooted mountain," "the joy of the whole earth," and "the mountains of Zion." Most remarkable of all, it tells how what was once "the sides of the north" has now become "the city of the great King," and "God is known in her towers." With these words it clearly points to the wonder that is the Church. The northern region of the earth belongs to what is shadowed and frozen. It stays dark forever and gets no share of the sun's rays, and for this reason the name "north" signifies the opposing power. So the one who once lived in the north and was its side has left the dark and frozen life and has become the city of God and the dwelling place of the kingdom. God is known in her towers. By "towers" he means the outlines of square buildings. Through this riddle he hints at the firm and lofty towers of virtue that can be seen in the souls of the saints, since God is known only by lives like these. What follows agrees with what has already been said. "For the kings were gathered together" in her, since that divine city is populated by a gathering of people who reign, not people who serve as slaves. "They saw it," it says, "and so they marvelled." It also explains the reason for their wonder. Those who had unworthily lived in this city when it was the side of the north "were troubled and shaken, and trembling seized them," and not only trembling but pains like those of a woman giving birth. All these things, it says, happened to them through the violent wind that shatters the ships of apostasy, which float wickedly on the sea of life. "With a violent wind," it says, "you will shatter the ships of Tarshish." Anyone who remembers the account in Acts knows about the violent blast that came to the disciples in the upper room. Anyone who has paid attention to the prophecy of Jonah knows that the one who runs from God looks for a ship sailing to Tarshish. Then the discourse is divided, as it were, between two persons. In the earlier part it takes the role of the one who foretells, and in what follows it speaks in the voices of those who received the word. Agreeing

with the truth of what came before, as if it had heard these things from someone else, it says: "As we have heard, so also we have seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God." So it also has those who joyfully saw what we had heard urge one another on. The exhortation was: "Go around Zion and embrace her; tell of her in her towers. Set your hearts on her strength, and survey her towers," along with what the passage goes on to say. After this, the proclamation of the word extends [?] in due order to the whole earth. Before the confusion of tongues all people had one lip and one voice, and so now too all the nations, the whole inhabited world and all people become one hearing and one heart, because the one Word sounds in all of them. Having gathered all human nature into one assembly and set the whole world around himself as a single theatre, he cries out his word to everyone together: "Hear, all you nations; give ear, all who inhabit the world, both earthborn and sons of men, whether any among us is rich or happens to be poor." With these three pairs he includes, in general terms, every difference in human [?] life. In the first pair he says "all nations" and "those who inhabit the world." The names of the nations signify the boundaries of places, and the phrase that follows means the people who live in those places. By saying "earthborn" and "sons of men," he separates the fleshly, earthy and more irrational people from those who are being saved and who bear some mark of human nature. The mark proper to a human being is likeness to the divine. Unequal lives of poverty and wealth are the most general cause of the many varied irregularities in human affairs. Who is this speaking to so great an audience? Who else but the one who testifies in the psalm that he will speak wisdom and understanding? The one who speaks these things is the one who has the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, [?] this great grace, which is achieved through attention and study. He did not say that he would open his mouth until he had bent his ear to the word set before him. "My mouth," he says, "shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding." First "I will bend my ear to a parable," and only then "I will open my riddle on the harp." What, then, is the understanding, and what is the riddle? God's creation, it says, knows of no making of an evil day [?], as the account of the world's creation bears witness. It was sin that turned the day of rejoicing into a day of fear and punishment. We could have been free from fearing that day if the serpent that watches for our heel, whose name is [iniquity?], had not wrapped its coil around the whole course of life,

bristling fearfully and rough on every side with the varied scales of the passions. Then he divides the whole psalm in two. In the first part he gives counsel not to look to any other redeemer. "A brother does not redeem," it says, "nor does any other man," but each must ransom himself, if he gives God an atonement for himself and the price of his soul's redemption. It wants this counsel to lead us to look down on the vain pursuits of this life. How do people spend their lives in senseless toil, as if they expected to live forever? How can they fail to expect the decay that death brings, when they see those who came before them dying? They are truly foolish and senseless, because they do not know that after this life they will leave their wealth to others while they themselves dwell in tombs forever. They did not write their names in heaven through the higher life. They longed to be famous on earth instead, and so they made themselves nameless in the city above. The cause of all this is that man does not understand his own honour. He lets himself be dragged down into bestial pleasures, handing himself over to the gullet, the belly and the filth that comes after the belly. That is the first division of the psalm. The rest makes the accusation in other terms, and the passage again ends with the same words. Here, I think, the prophecy teaches us a lesson: the first cause of the entry of evils is that man is made into a beast by the more animal passions. Grace healed us of this evil through the one who visited humankind in compassion. Yet people again abandon the good shepherd and are shepherded by death. They turn themselves not toward the heavenly pasture but toward the pasture in Hades, and become sheep of Hades. For it says, "Like sheep they are laid in Hades; death shall shepherd them." So for a second time, through sin, people become blind to the honour given us by grace and sink down into the irrational life. Everything that happens outside the true Word is irrationality, and irrationality and senselessness are what mark a beast.

Chapter 13. It would be pointless to write out every detail of the psalms precisely, word by word, because anyone who wishes can easily understand the parts I have left out from what has already been said. So I do not think I need to lengthen this discourse with many words. Only one point from what was examined earlier needs to be repeated: great David benefits human nature in two ways. He symbolically prefigures our salvation, and he shows people how to repent, applying a kind of art to this achievement through

the fiftieth psalm, by which another victory over the adversary is prepared for us. Knowing how to cleanse ourselves of evils is the preparation and foundation for lasting victory over the enemy. Throughout life our wrestling against the world-ruler of this darkness and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places never stops, and we have only one counter-hold against every attack of temptation, namely repentance. So whoever has achieved repentance in himself always wins against the one who keeps on wrestling with him. After this, the historical events in the headings are out of order, but the meaning follows its proper sequence. The affair of Bathsheba and Uriah happened long after the story of Doeg the Edomite. The Doeg story took place at the beginning of Saul's tyranny, and the Bathsheba affair shortly before the end of David's reign. But the Spirit does not care about the chronological, fleshly order of events. What great benefit would I get from learning first about the Edomite and then being taught about Bathsheba? What virtue would come of it? What climb toward the better? What teaching that leads to lofty desires? But suppose I have learned the mysteries of the fiftieth psalm, everything its words contain at a deeper level, and with it I have been taught the remedy given to us for destroying the adversary, the word of repentance, so that through it I am always becoming used to victory over the enemy and practised in it. Then see how I go on in proper order to the next step of the ascent, gaining victory upon victory. I will read you the historical heading, which runs as follows: "For the end, of understanding, for David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul and said to him, 'David has come into the house of Abimelech.'" This teaches me that one comes to the goal of victory when understanding guides one's life, as it did for great David. And I grieve Doeg, the tyrant over my salvation, most of all when I am in the priest's house. Then the keeper of mules can no longer grapple with me face to face, so he secretly plots against me and informs the one who seeks my death that I am staying with the priest. It should be clear what the mules are over which this Edomite is in charge. He herds a sterile kind, in which God's blessing found no place, the blessing that from the beginning gave creation the power to multiply when God said, "Increase and multiply." The multiplying of evil does not come from God, just as mules do not come from one another in succession. Instead nature [?] always produces them anew, slipping in by its own trickery something that does not exist in creation. From what has been said it is clear what the text is aiming at. For if everything the Lord made is very

good, and the mule is not on the list of things made in creation, then clearly the account uses this name to point to evil. Evil does not get its existence from God, and once it comes into being as it does, it does not last in a substance of its own. The mule cannot reproduce itself, and in the same way evil does not keep itself in existence forever. It must always be brought to life by something else, whenever the noble, proud, swift and high-necked [?] part of our nature slides through desire into a senseless [?] and irrational union. So that foreigner Doeg, who acted as Saul's messenger against David and herded the sterile drove of mules, can be none other than the evil angel, who drags the human soul toward evil through the [?] passions of sin. When he sees that a person is in the house of the true priest and finds he cannot strike him with the mules' kicks, he informs against him to the ruler of wickedness, the spirit now at work in the sons of disobedience. But the one rooted like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God speaks against the tyrant the words we heard in the psalm: "Why do you boast in evil, you who are mighty in lawlessness, whose tongue is like a sharpened razor?" This tongue strips the beauty of the hair from those it is applied to and cuts off the seven locks of hair in which our strength lies. You surely grasp what the seven spiritual locks mean, since Isaiah listed the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. When these are cut off, as happened to Samson, the loss of the eyes follows, and one becomes a laughingstock to the foreigners when they are drunk. After describing the traits of the one who is mighty in evil, he adds that "God will destroy him in the end," and meanwhile, now, "will pluck him out and remove him from" the divine "tabernacle," and will dig up the roots of his wickedness and bitterness from the land of the living. The rest of the psalm looks to the same meaning. Through all this, those "rooted in faith," as the divine Apostle said, gain steadfastness. "For I," it says, "like a fruitful olive tree in the house of my God, have hoped in the mercy of God forever," and beyond that, for the span whose measure is infinity, which he calls "forever and ever." In this hope he promises to give thanks to God for all eternity: "I will give thanks to you forever, for you have done for me what deserves thanksgiving. And I will wait for your name," for patient waiting is good for your holy ones. A many-coloured gleam shifts unnoticed from one shade to another in the varying bloom of a dye, the edges of each colour's brightness blending naturally into one another. In the same way one can

see the ray of meaning at the edge of this psalm blending in sequence with the opening brilliance of the psalm beside it. The boundary between them passes unnoticed, and the thought flows of its own accord from this psalm into the next. Consider the one who is rooted like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God. He has made the firm and immovable foundation of faith secure in himself, and through thanksgiving he has stretched out his hope of the divine oil across the infinity of the ages. This person turns his anger against fools, whose chief folly is to say that he who truly is, who is over all and in all, does not exist. Since things are as they are, he says (he first shows God's providence for humankind, in which the steadfastness of our hopes is so unchangeable that our longing, stretching out with the eternity of the ages, does not grow weary), how can "the fool say in his heart, 'There is no God'"? "They are corrupt and have become abominable" in such pursuits of the mind. Falling away from what truly is, is truly corruption and the breaking apart of what holds together. How could anyone have being who is not in him who is? And how could anyone remain in him who is without believing that he who is exists? He who truly is, is certainly God, as the vision of the theophany given to great Moses testifies. So whoever drives the being of God out of his own mind by saying that God does not exist has destroyed his own being, because he has placed himself outside of being. That is why it says that since they turned away from God, "they all at once became worthless," like a discarded vessel judged useless. Something useless for good clearly shows that it is fit for evil, because it is unsuited to what is better. For these reasons, then, the Lord "looked down from heaven on the sons of men." These words foretell the Lord's life among people, when the whole body of the people followed the priests, Pharisees and scribes who led the way into unbelief. They were the ones who tore and devoured the people with their blasphemous teeth. That is why it says, "There they were afraid with fear where there was no fear, those who eat up my people as they eat bread." They suffer something like the condition of people with hydrophobia. If such sufferers could somehow take in water, it would cure their condition. But in some way they fear the very thing offered for their salvation and turn away from what saves them, and so in their fear of perishing they bring about their own destruction. So it was with those men. The spring cried out to them, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink." But the madness of unbelief had already seized the senses of their souls, and they were afraid with fear where there was no fear. They turned away from the drink of salvation, not knowing that God is in the generation of the righteous, the God who gives salvation to Israel out of Zion and the captivity of the people

…his [?]. Turning back again to himself from the one who wickedly took us captive through sin, when [?], the true Israelite and spiritual Jacob comes to be in gladness and rejoicing. Such, then, is the sense of the psalm, as one can discover from the progression of its words. And the inscription of the psalm agrees with this sense. For the inscription indicates that the content of the psalm is a victory song, performed through dancing with understanding: "To the end," it says, "for Maeleth," which is translated "through dancing." And in place of "to the end" others among the translators have rendered "victory song." Again, as the discourse advances through what follows, it fits the riddles of the history to the thoughts that are found as one progresses. This happens when that Doeg the Idumean, who pastured within himself the ambiguous nature of mules, is made powerless against us. It was also said in what came before that sin is signified by this animal. Sin is the fruit of that ambiguous tree which the Word calls good and evil. It is good because sin is veiled by the bait of pleasure, which the lovers of the body pursue in place of the good. But it is evil in turn, because what is now eagerly pursued as good ends in a bitter outcome. In the same way, one can see in the animal in question the marks of each nature, horse and donkey. The mule is at once horse and donkey, not each separately but two in one, since the double nature of the two animals has been blended to produce it. That foreigner whom we have recognized informs the tyrant of our stay with the priest. Then we, by divine alliance, cast down from his power the one who boasts in wickedness and holds his power in lawlessness, and tear him up root and all from the land of the living. We become an olive tree, laden and exulting in an abundance of fruit, and strengthened by hope in God we dance victory songs over the defeated one. When this happens, we advance in due order to higher things, truly, as the voice in the Song says, "leaping over the mountains and bounding over the hills." What, then, is this mountain to which the discourse now leaps from the former mountain of thoughts? Another victory again, and other hymns for that victory, achieved by David with understanding. Those who stir up the contests are no longer a herd of mules but the nation of the Ziphites. They sit guarding the narrows of the parched passage, and when they cannot prevent our journey through the narrow place, they [?] the one who is grieved at our salvation. For "To the end," it says, "of understanding, in hymns, for David, when the Ziphites came and

said to Saul, 'Behold, David is hidden among us.'" Anyone who knows the history is surely aware that a narrow and parched place is mentioned in this part of it. By the narrowed passage we understood the gospel road of the kingdom. The Ziphites obstruct this road, that is, the foreign nation of demons, the servants of the opposing power; but the few who turn away from the broad road find it. The wording of the history runs thus: "Is not David hidden in Masera among us, in the narrows on the hill?" For truly those who live according to God hide themselves in this narrow way. The New Testament shows us this way, by which one can climb to the topmost summit of the mountain, which the account of the history calls a hill. So when we pass through that narrow way unhindered, the Ziphites inform the tyrant of our salvation. But we ascribe the power of our judgment in favour of the good to the name of the one who has saved us, saying, "O God, save me by your name, and by your power you will judge me." For the text casts what has already happened in the form of something still expected, and in this way Scripture disregards precision about time. Prophecy often relates what will be as though it were past, and what has happened as though it were expected. One can see this in this psalm too, toward the end. For it did not say, "my eye will look upon my enemies," but "my eye has looked." From this we learn that for God nothing is past, but all things are in the present. So even if the words convey some sense of past and future concerning the divine power, the meaning does not leave the present. The one who has set foot on the parched and narrow way, and has put the band of Ziphites to flight, therefore says to God: "Our salvation has come about in your name, and the judgment in favour of the good has its strength in your power, and so it will be forever." And for these things he calls on the divine ear to listen to his thanksgiving. He tells of the uprising of strangers, and of how those mighty in wickedness sought his soul. These are not led by God but by the one understood to be his adversary. That is why he says that they "did not set God before them," "but God helps me." God turns evils back upon the inventors of wickedness, "and by his truth destroys" everything that is hostile and foreign to the truth. "But I," he says, "will give thanks to the name by which I was saved, because thanksgiving is good. For I have come out of my afflictions, and with my own eyes I have looked upon the destruction of my enemies." The prophetic eye rejoices at this, when nothing contrary to virtue is seen any longer. For when wickedness, which sets itself against virtue in the rank of an enemy, has been removed, not even the name of enemies will remain. For how will anyone still be called an enemy when that enmity no longer

exists, which peace has slain, as the Apostle says? To see how the thoughts stated fit consistently with the words of the psalm, read the psalm itself word for word: it is the one placed fifty-third in the sequence. When he has already prevailed over the Ziphites and seen the utter destruction of wickedness, he again takes his stand in understanding of the alliance from above and offers God a victory hymn. For this is what the text of the inscription contains: "To the end, in hymns of understanding, for David." In bodily contests, athletes do not stay with the same opponents they defeated in the wrestling school in their youth. As their strength grows, they strip for bigger and stronger rivals, and if they defeat these, they dust themselves for bouts against superior ones, always taking on more powerful opponents as their strength increases. In the same way, [?] the one who has been trained by so many victories over enemies makes his victories more glorious by grappling with more glorious and greater antagonists. And for this reason he calls on the ear of the judge of the contest, saying, "Give ear, O God, to my prayer, and do not disregard my supplication." He also asks him to attend to his contest, saying, "Attend to me and hear me." And through his words he shows the labours of the contests, recounting grief and idle talk, trouble of heart, the voice of the enemy and the affliction of the sinner. In this way he shows the judge of the contest, as it were, the wrestling holds his antagonists are applying to him. Besides these, he tells of trouble of heart, cowardice before death, fear and trembling, and darkness covering his whole life. Against all of these he found one device to rise above and beyond so great a distress: to be given wings, the swift feathers of the dove, and, once airborne, to end his flight in that place which is empty of all evils and flourishing [?] with things more divine. "For having lodged," he says, "in the wilderness," away from the faint-heartedness below and from the storm of temptations, he would there receive God's salvation, where wickedness is destroyed. For "drowning" means destruction, since everything that has gone into the deep disappears. So the drowning and ruin of sin is the dissolving of the structure of wickedness. That is why he says that evil is drowned by God when the tongues of those who conspire in evil are divided. And everything that the sense of this psalm contains after this, the description of the city populated by evil practices, all looks to the same end. For he speaks of the evil inhabitants of this city and lists them,

naming lawlessness and contradiction, which go round the wall of the city by night, and again lawlessness, toil and injustice, which are nurtured in the middle of the town. He also shows the evil populace that fills its streets, naming usury and deceit. And the heaviest of all these, he says, is hypocrisy, which puts on the guise of like-mindedness and affection and hides deceit under a kindly veil. For this reason the just judge sends in settlers worthy of such inhabitants. Do you want to learn the names of the settlers? "Let death come upon them," he says, "and let them go down alive into Hades." And having shown in his discourse all the grim things concerning them, he adds the sweet [?] … the full company, saying, "But I will hope in you." By the full company of this city he means "men of blood and deceit," who do not halve any kind of evil day and do not show their wickedness incomplete, but have perfection in evil. He becomes the victor over all of them with this one utterance, by which he reveals his disposition toward God, saying, "But I will hope

CHAPTER 14. Having gone through these thoughts, let the diligent reader read the inspired words of the psalm for himself. That way we will not burden him by setting everything out word for word and prolonging the contemplation of each thought. Think of those who are climbing a steep and difficult road. When they come upon a seat halfway and rest from their long and strenuous toil, their strength is renewed, and they rouse themselves again to climb to the heights above.
