So too the traveller on the road of virtue, whose crowns are victories over his opponents, as the inscription of the previous psalm testifies, braces himself with the success of his victory and strains again toward what lies above. For great too was the struggle he overcame in the psalm just mentioned: grief, idle talk, trouble, enmity and hearing (for that is what "the voice of the enemy" means), the affliction that comes from sinners, and the wrath of those who bear grudges. Through these come trouble of mind, cowardice before death, fear, trembling, darkness and the like. He prevailed over opponents of this kind and number on the wing of the dove that appeared in life, and he moved away from those who grow wild in wickedness to the wilderness that is free of the growth of the tares of wickedness, where rest comes about. There he conquered a whole city of adversaries together with the full company of its inhabitants. Its inhabitants are lawlessness, toil, contradiction, usury, deceit, death and the descent of the living into Hades. Worst of all is the kind that always dwells there, hypocrisy, which works treachery under a show of like-mindedness. He overcomes this city by extending his trust in the divine through the whole time of his own life. For by saying evening and morning and noon, he takes in the whole measure of the day, in

which he says these things, and God consents to listen to them. God redeems his life in peace from those who draw near to him in a great company, whom he calls "men of blood" and "of deceit," and perfect in wickedness. He has prevailed over so many such enemies by hoping in God. Then again, as if forgetting the labours just shown, he rouses himself against stronger and greater antagonists. See what kind of labour he takes on himself through these contests: "For the people," it says, "who have been removed far from the holy ones." This people is the whole human race. Separation from the holy commandments has walled it off from God by a vast and boundless distance. He calls this people back through his victory over the adversary, making the salvation of the lost the prize of his contests. For this reason his achievement is engraved on a pillar in writing that cannot be erased, so that the memory of what happened endures forever. So David's victory becomes "an inscription for a pillar," "when," it says, "the foreigners seized him in Gath." So that the meaning woven into the text through the riddles of the history does not escape us, I will run briefly through the history. Envy against David grew up in the tyrannical Saul over the victory against Goliath, because of the acclaim of those who celebrated the victory with dancing. Saul plotted David's murder by every means, secretly and openly: now he contrived plots in secret, now he took up arms openly and stirred up his subjects against him. Saul made attempt after attempt on David, and in the end David went to the Gittites. He lived in one of the foreigners' cities, which they willingly gave up to him, and stayed there with his comrades in arms. He lived with two lawful wives. One of them was an Israelite. The other had been the wife of one of the powerful men around Carmel, and after his death she married David. Such is the content

So the statement that he was "seized" among the foreigners does not signify that he was arrested to be harmed, for that is not what happened. It signifies loving kindness and goodwill, for the Gittites settled among themselves the man who had been driven from his ancestral land. What then? Did this David, the son of Jesse, a man born of men, achieve so much by his own contests that he called back the whole of human nature, which had been removed far from God by transgressing the holy commandments, and revealed to it the riddles of the pillar-inscription? (Anyone who calls the inspired Scripture a pillar-inscription will not be wrong.) Or is it clear from the way the history fits together that the one this great is he who went out beyond the borders of Judea, founded a city for himself among foreigners, and found rest in a double marriage,

receiving into his bridal chamber one wife of Israelite race and the other from the foreigners? So if the account of this must be laid bare more clearly, this is the one who is at once victor and bridegroom. For through the deeds by which he defeated the one who has the power of death, he, the one mighty in war, rescued into freedom this countless people held fast in Hades. And when the Israelite people rushed in envy and jealousy to murder him, he is "seized" with goodwill by the foreigners. He establishes a city among them, by which I mean the Church, and in it he strengthens his kingdom. It was he who said to those ranked under Saul, "The kingdom will be taken from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits." In this city there is indeed something of Israelite nobility too, according to the prophetic utterance that says, "In the assemblies bless God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel." For those who began the word of faith, the heralds of the truth, the founders of the Church (I mean the disciples and apostles) came from the fountains of Israel. "The princes of Judah," it says, "their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali." Through certain signs and symbols the prophecy foreshadows the distinctive features of the disciples' race. Among them is also "the younger Benjamin," instructed in the mysteries "in ecstasy": Paul the divine apostle, of the seed of Abraham and the tribe of Benjamin. Yet although the king is recorded as living with the Israelite woman, Abigail is loved more. She had once lived with Nabal the Carmelite, surnamed "the Cynic," that harsh man of the mountains, the shearer of sheep. When he was destroyed, the woman lived with the king and became the mother of kings. So the inscription of the psalm contains all these mysteries. It points to the people removed far from the holy ones, and to the pillar set up for the achievements on behalf of the foreigners. Through the letters on it, this pillar stands as a reproach to those who share the unbelief of the Jews, but as guidance toward the good and an example to those saved through faith. The words of the psalm themselves, however, seem somehow to look not so much to the king who has appeared as to David himself, the contestant against wickedness and the worker of virtue. Yet no one would say that the thoughts of the psalm are out of tune with the riddles of the inscription. For one who looks to theology truly and in the proper way will certainly show a life in harmony with his faith. And this happens in no other way than when the uprising of the flesh has been brought down by the practices of virtue. The sum of virtue is God's alliance, and he is deemed worthy of it who makes the divine oil [?] his own through his life. Suppose a robber or a murderer suddenly attacked someone, and he called on some of his friends for help, not being

able on his own to escape the danger. So here too, being in the struggle, he calls on help from above because of his grappling with "man." (By saying "man" he uses the comprehensive term to indicate the passions of nature.) He says that he is trampled by the one who wars against him, and that he is worn out and crushed by a battle that lasts all day. For the one grappling with him in these contests is not just one: the one "man" is a whole host of enemies. "For my enemies trampled me," he says, "all day long," striking from on high, because they have got above the one being trampled. And what happens does not happen by day or in the light, for then I would not have been afraid, with the light as my ally. That is why he says, "I shall not fear by day," implying without saying it that his enemies bring fear upon him through the darkness. But such a man makes day for himself by hoping in the light, through which the darkness is destroyed. "I shall not fear by day; but I will hope in you." Perhaps one would grasp the sense of what is written better by looking at the riddle of the inscription. For as long as the human people was far from the holy angels, it was trampled by the passions of nature, worn out and crushed by the unending war, struck from above, and gripped by fear in the night. But when it hoped in God, shaking off like a burden the hope that had strayed after vain things, then it praised its own words, which are the confession of faith. "In God," it says, "I will praise my words." But my enemies, he says, abhor these praiseworthy words. They devise plans against me for evil and contrive hidden, concealed treachery while living close by. They make this their particular practice and never stop watching my heel. For this has been the work of the man-slayer from the beginning: to watch the heel of man. But even if the enemies' attack is heavy, they will be driven back by your alliance, since salvation comes to human beings from you freely, not from works of righteousness but from your grace alone. "For you will save them for nothing." And the whole sequence of the psalm, in order, explains the recalling of human nature. Its sum is the indelible record of the victory over the adversary. It is a memorial of God's love for humanity, as if on a pillar, set before all creation as a theme for giving glory. That is why he says in the last part of the psalm, looking to this pillar: "In God I will praise a word, in the Lord I will praise a saying; in God I have hoped." Because of him I no longer fear the fear of the flesh. "And in me," he says, "are vows, which I will render with praise. For you have rescued my soul from death,

"and my feet from slipping." By "slipping" he means turning aside from the path we walk by way of the commandments, which is how the fall came about. So, freed from death and raised up from the fall, he comes before the face of God. He had fled from God when he first ate of what the commandment forbade, and had hidden himself for shame in the shade of the fig tree. Having regained his freedom of speech, then, he is restored to the living light. "For I will be pleasing," he says, "to the Lord in the light of the living", the light from which he had been estranged at the beginning through sin. That is enough on these matters. I do not think one should examine each detail too laboriously and so stretch the discourse beyond measure. There are many victory psalms among the sacred hymns, as the inscription "for the end" shows, and in them the victory over our adversaries is seen in many ways. But the victory over those who wrestle against us that is signified through the riddles of history seems to have a meaning of its own. I mean the history that recounts the affairs of Saul. In it the order of the psalms was not arranged according to the sequence of historical events. Instead it followed those who are being perfected by progress in virtue. It fitted each thing revealed in the events to show the corresponding growth in virtue, so that first and last are set in sequence according to the principle of virtue, and the order is not enslaved to the material chance of events. That is why the encounter in the cave is interpreted after many events, though it happened before many of them: the meeting of Saul, who was pursuing to kill, and David, who was trying to avoid being killed. In that encounter the power to kill was turned the other way round. The man pursued to his death stood over the slaughter of his murderer. He had the power to punish his enemy, and the strength as well as the power, yet he held back the punishment and killed his own anger within himself instead of the enemy. The facts of the history are surely plain to all who do not study divine things as a side matter. Still, we will tell it briefly, condensing the narrative as much as we can. There was a desert place in Judea where David, being pursued and at a loss what to do, was camping. In it there was a spacious cave, which admitted those who went down into it through a single mouth. While Saul was searching for David and scouring the desert with his whole army, David and his men were forced to take refuge in the cave. When they were already inside, Saul also came within the mouth after them in order to attend to a need of nature. He did not know of the stratagem against his safety that had arisen of its own accord. So he was by himself, and he took off his cloak and laid it down somewhere beside him. The light from the mouth made him visible to those hidden within in the darkness. All the others with David were minded to rush upon the enemy and take vengeance on the man who had come to murder them, as though God had given

the enemy into the hands of those pursued to their deaths. But David forbade them to act on their impulse, for he judged it unlawful to make an attempt on their king. He bared his sword from its sheath and stood secretly behind Saul, so that his attempt against him had no witness, since the darkness in the cave hid it from sight and kept what was happening from being exposed. He could have driven the whole sword with a single blow through Saul's back into his heart. Yet he neither touched Saul's body nor meant to. Instead, without Saul noticing, he cut off the edge of the cloak with the sword, so that the cloak might afterward bear witness to his kindness toward Saul, since the cut edge showed that he had had the power to strike Saul's body. This made clear how well David had been trained in long-suffering. He held a bare sword in his hand, his enemy's body lay under his hand, and it was in his power to kill. Yet he conquered anger by reason and the power to strike by the fear of God. He not only mastered his own anger, but also restrained his armor-bearer, who had rushed to kill Saul, with that celebrated cry: "Do not destroy the Lord's anointed." So Saul came out of the cave knowing nothing of what had happened, and wrapped the cut cloak around himself. David came out behind him, taking care for his own safety, and went ahead to the hillock above the cave, where he held out the edge of the cloak in his hand. This was nothing other than a bloodless trophy over his adversaries. He shouted to Saul in a loud voice and recounted this novel and wonderful feat of valor, which no gore of blood had stained, in which the champion won and the defeated man came away safe. For David's valor is not attested by the fall of his enemy. Rather, by saving his opponent from danger he shows the superiority of his strength all the more clearly. He had such confidence that he did not stake his own safety on the destruction of those arrayed against him, but felt secure even while those plotting against him were alive, as though no one were troubling him. Or rather, the word teaches this through the history: the one who excels in virtue shows his courage not against his own kin but against the passions. So through this feat of David's the anger in both men was slain. David overcame his own wrath by reason and [?] the anger bent on retaliation; Saul put to death his malice against David through the kindness shown him. What Saul afterward says to the victor, sinking down in shame at what he had dared and showing by lament and tears that he had inwardly turned from his wickedness, can be learned from the history itself. Such, then, is the subject of the fifty-sixth psalm, as far as the history reveals it. The words of the inscription itself, which point to the encounter in the cave, run as follows: "For the end. Do not destroy. Of David, for an inscription on a pillar,

when he fled from the face of Saul into the cave." Now it is time to consider briefly how the thoughts of the psalm fit what is inscribed, and to contemplate their meaning, after first going through the divinely inspired words. "Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul has trusted in you, and in the shadow of your wings I will hope, until lawlessness passes away." The Psalmist asks that divine mercy be given him in return for his trust in God and his firm hope in him, "until," he says, "lawlessness passes away." To make the meaning clearer, let us take up the passage this way. The nature of sin is unstable and transient. It was not brought into being along with creation at the beginning by the one who gave all things their being and substance, and it does not endure forever along with the things that are. For what comes from Being exists and remains in being forever. But if something lies outside Being, and its existence consists not in being but in not being good, this is the grass on the housetops, rootless, unsown and unploughed. Even if for now it is a nuisance with its insubstantial growth, at the appointed times, in the restoration of all things to the good, it passes away and vanishes. No trace of the evil that now covers our surface will be left in the life laid up for us in hope. "For yet a little while," he says, "and the sinner will be no more, and you will look for his place and will not

So at the opening of the psalm the word philosophizes in lofty doctrines, explaining the nature of evil. It teaches that we need mercy as our ally until the lawlessness that wickedly took up residence in life passes out of our life. Such an alliance is granted us when we trust in the power of our ally and arm ourselves with the shadow of God's wings. Anyone who takes the shadow of the divine wings, which becomes a covering for us, to mean the virtues will not go wrong. For the Divine itself, whatever it is by nature, remains unattainable and incomprehensible to human nature, soaring somewhere far above in its ineffability, beyond the reach of human reasoning. But an imprint of that ineffable nature arises for those who look toward it through the shadowy outline of the virtues. So all wisdom and prudence and knowledge, and every approach of thought that seeks to comprehend, are not the divine wings themselves but the shadow of the divine wings. This shadow is a great benefit to us. "For I will cry," he says, "to God Most High, to God who has done me good", through this shadow, which he sent from on high to life below. He saved me through the Spirit who overshadowed in the cloud, and he has now turned those who trampled on me in the earlier psalms about into the ranks of those who are reproached. "For God sent forth his mercy

and his truth, and rescued my soul from the midst of lion cubs." Truly my sins were once cubs to me, lion cubs that tore me with their fearsome jaws and sharp claws. But allies came, mercy and truth, that fair pair. For mercy is not without judgment, nor is truth without mercy. Through them I am freed from living among these cubs. These beasts, he says, are "sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword." The constitution of our nature knows nothing of such physical members set in human mouths in place of teeth. But when someone becomes like the passion and is transformed to match the wickedness that rules him, he loses his natural form and becomes a beast. That is why, having mentioned lions, he named the sons of men, whose teeth and tongue are instruments of war. So the one who has been lifted so high in mind that he lodges under the shadow of the divine wings, and is taken up from earth to the heavenly lot ("For he sent from heaven," he says, "and saved me"), no longer looks to earthly things but busies himself with the glory in the heavens, saying: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth." And describing the assaults of his enemies, he says they are caught in their own evils and fall into their own pits. For he says: "They prepared a snare for my feet and bowed down my soul; they dug a pit before my face and fell into it." He himself, he says, is ready to sing the divine glory in praise. How blessed that man is for such greatness of soul! His heart is prepared to praise the divine glory, containing within itself the One who cannot be contained. He says that he is prepared and ready. He does not put off the song but summons his living instruments, calling them by name to the service of hymnody: "Awake, psaltery and lyre." This shows the harmonious concord of the twofold man, visible and hidden, in glorifying God, and the instruments obey the one who calls them. The time for such music is dawn, for the glory of God is not awakened in those who have not put off the works of darkness. "I will awake at dawn," say the psaltery and lyre to the one who calls them. And so he promises to render to God thanksgiving, which he calls confession, rendered among peoples and nations. The grace of faith is divided equally between these two names, the peoples and the nations. For God is not the God of the Jews only, but of the gentiles too, "since God is one, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith." Therefore, since the divine blessing has been poured out on both like a double stream, divided partly to the peoples and partly to the nations,

the prophecy offers God thanksgiving on behalf of both. For though sin had grown without limit, God's mercy surpasses it in its own greatness and rises even above the height of heaven. "For great," he says, "above the heavens is your mercy." I think the words of praise for these things are the closing words of the psalm, where he says: "Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth." For the more the glorifying of God abounds on earth, increased by those saved through faith, the more the powers beyond the world rejoice at our salvation and hymn and glorify God. So the heavenly host spoke to the shepherds when the angels saw on earth the peace that had appeared in our life because of God's good pleasure among men: "Glory to God in the highest."

CHAPTER 15. The psalm that follows surpasses the height of this one in greatness, as much as one can learn from what is written. Among runners, the one who outruns the winner of the others wins greater glory than the first and is shown to be better than the one who ran ahead. In the same way the fifty-seventh psalm seems to surpass the preceding one in the grandeur of its thoughts, although that one has been shown to be great in meaning. As that one carried off the prize over the others, so this one outdoes the psalm that excelled the others, for the inscription "For the end" bears witness to victory in this one too. But here the word seems to attest not so much the defeat of the adversaries as the abundance of good things in this victory. The wording of the inscription is this: "For the end. Do not destroy. Of David, for an inscription on a pillar." How many times the contestant in long-suffering is proclaimed for the crown of this victory by the president of the games himself! Perhaps the Holy Spirit takes up this phrase again and again in admiration, since it lies beyond human power and exceeds the bounds of nature. Only the incorporeal and immaterial nature, to which no human passion clings, could say such a thing. But David was a man, with anger inborn in his nature. He suffered ill from a man who had been given no occasion for evil, and who had been granted many great benefits, both in the matter of his empty rule and in what had been done for that very man. Yet David was made an exile by the very man who had received his kindness, and a fugitive from his own hearth, hunted to death by the one he had treated well. At a loss what to do, he went now to one place and now to another. He camped in deserts, fled to mountain heights, became a suppliant of foreigners, suffered in want of necessities, and endured mostly in the open air. He often faced mortal danger from Saul: once when Saul himself rushed at him with a spear to kill him, and again when Saul surrounded the house where he was staying with spearmen, so that he would not escape death.

Then Saul made meddlesome inquiries everywhere: with whom David lodged and with whom he ate, at whose house he was staying, and to whom he moved on. And twice the chance to kill his enemy came David's way. Once Saul unexpectedly fell into David's hands in the cave; again it was at the tent, when Saul was overcome by sleep and David stood over him as he slept, and he was free to vent all his anger by killing his pursuer. Yet he neither laid a hand on him himself, and to the man who was eager to kill him he said: "Do not destroy." This voice is plainly God's, forbidding the destruction of a human being. Those who want to make inscriptions on stone stand out more cut the shapes of the letters deep with the chisel, running the tool over the impressions many times. In the same way, by continual repetition the Holy Spirit makes this great saying stand out more clearly and distinctly on the pillar of our memory, so that the writing, imprinted on us clearly and without blurring, may be read in times of suffering. For I think the Holy Spirit's dispensation aims at this: that the achievements of holy men who went before should be set out to guide later life, so that imitation may lead us to an equal and similar good. When the soul swells with the desire to take revenge on the one provoking it, and the blood around the heart boils with anger against the one who has hurt it, let someone then look up to this pillar which the Holy Spirit set up for David and read the saying on it, which David uttered on behalf of his murderer. He will surely calm the turmoil of thoughts in his soul and soothe his passion through the longing to imitate such deeds. Through the very words of the psalm one can also see the greatness of the one who has climbed by progress to the step of this psalm, and how far he has risen above the greatness of the one before. For he no longer complains of being trampled by his enemies, nor calls on mercy as his ally. Having risen above, as if from a high lookout, he cries out in reproof to those living below in the hollows of the foothills of human life, saying something like this: "O men, what are you saying and doing? Is what you say justice? Do you judge with uprightness? But I see that your hearts are on the earth, and every movement of the heart is a deed and not just a thought. For as soon as evil takes shape in the mind, the deed is woven together with the thoughts through the hands." I have set this out for clarity, paraphrasing the psalm's wording a little. The words themselves run as follows: "If truly you speak justice, judge uprightly, sons of men. For in your heart you work lawlessness on the earth; your hands weave injustice together." Then, lamenting over those who have fallen away from salvation, he adds the words that follow: "The sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly." You would understand this saying if you examined what the first

womb of human existence is, and what belly conceived humankind. I think it is none other than God's love for humanity and his goodness, by which we were fashioned and born. For he said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," he who "fashioned their hearts one by one." And again he says, "I have begotten sons and raised them up, but they have rejected me." One can gather countless such sayings from Holy Scripture, which show what belly fashioned us and what mother brought us into the light by birth. Looking to these, then, the one who grieves over the ruin of those who have fallen away mourns, for the voice in which he bewails the sinners is plainly a dirge: "How have the sinners been estranged from the womb? How have they gone astray from the belly," honoring the lie above the truth, these men whose anger resembles that of the first father of the lie? "Like that of an asp," he says, "deaf and stopping its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor be drugged with a drug by a wise man." Those expert in such matters have observed this trait of the beast: when it is inflamed with anger it holds its breath in its throat and does not let it out, swelling like a wineskin as it holds in its breath. So all the charms for beasts that such experts have discovered through some natural antipathy stay idle and useless against it. By this he gives us to understand that the heart of those held fast by wickedness stays deaf to the healing their teachers apply to them. The whole course of the psalm proceeds as a lament by one who groans over the ruin of the wretched. For he foretells what will happen to them, saying: "God will crush their teeth in their mouth." Which teeth? Clearly the ones that ate in disobedience, the servants of the belly's pleasures (which he called weapons and arrows in the preceding psalm), by which the word of truth is torn apart. "And the Lord has shattered the molars of the lions," he says. You would know whom he called lions if you learned the traits of these beasts. For they say that lions have distorted eyes, that their nature is carnivorous and fond of blood [?]. You surely know the riddle in the distortion of the eyes: it refers to those who do not look straight. And the foulness of their breath refers to those who have used their mouth for blasphemy and are therefore akin to the stench of sin. And as for what is understood through the breath [?], that flesh and blood, which most of all nourish the lions' nature, these [?] God's kingdom. For at the time when the worthy are honored, "these," he says, "will be brought to nothing," flowing away together with the unstable nature of the material things they made their own during life. "For they will be brought to nothing," he says, "like water running past." For the wicked archer who aims at our souls, who [shoots] the fiery arrows of sin against human

…the one who directs life does not stop shooting at them until he has cut the sinews of their strength. “For he will bend his bow,” it says, “until they grow weak.” And they become like melting wax, easily moulded into every form of sin’s stamp. To this he further adds those mournful cries against the wretched: “Fire fell,” he says, “and they did not see the sun.” Another of the translators makes the sense of this verse clear by rendering the untimely slipping of a miscarried child from the womb in these words: “A woman’s miscarriage,” he says, “will not behold the sun.” Now at the beginning of the psalm he says, “Sinners were estranged from the womb, and went astray from the belly,” which is the same as saying they were miscarried, and he names as the cause of this condition their likeness to the serpent and the asp. So now he takes up the same thought again and says that, having become incomplete by the standard of nature and miscarried through wickedness, they slipped out and fell from that womb which we have understood spiritually, becoming a fire against themselves through their material choice; and for this reason they did not look up at the sun. By the sun he points to the true light, to which the unripe offspring of the Jews did not look up. The next verse also fits in sequence with what precedes. What he there called a deaf asp he now changes and calls an uncomprehending thorn; for understanding comes from hearing, and whoever does not receive the hearing inevitably throws away understanding along with it. So, just as there he first used the more general name of serpent and then added the most bitter species of that kind of beast, the asp, so here too he first sets out the name of thorn as a kind of genus and then adds the more vicious species among thorns, the buckthorn, whose points are sharp, whose spikes stand close together, and whose scratches harm those who come near and fester like poison. “But even if you are a thorn,” he says, “even if the buckthorn among thorns, so that you still think you are alive” (for one who does not have the true life does not truly live), “wrath will swallow you up.” Just as the life of sinners is not truly what it is called but is only so named (for what is cut off from true life is not life), so too with God: wrath, even if it seems so to sinners and is called so by them, is not wrath at all, but is “as wrath” to those who give this name to the requital paid back in accordance with God’s justice. This, then, is the meaning of “as though living” and “as in wrath he will swallow you up”: you are not in true life, and he is not truly seen to be in wrath. Then he says, “The righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” Not as one gloating over those [?], but as one who sets his own lot side by side with theirs; then he will call himself blessed for his good counsel, because he was not among those on whom he sees the vengeance taken on sinners. For he will see the purity of his own

hands all the better by comparing it with the gore of sinners. “He will wash his hands,” it says, “in the blood of the sinner.” Now we know that we wash for no other reason than to rinse away dirt with water; but the stain of blood does not clean away dirt already there; it becomes dirt itself. So just as the colour white stands out more clearly when set against blood, so the purity of the righteous man’s hands is made more brilliant by comparison with its opposite. For what is now disbelieved, that those who have willingly suffered hardship through the labours of virtue have some share in what is better, will then be made plain by experience. Whoever sees these things will say, “So there was, it seems, a fruit stored up for the righteous in the righteous judgment of God.” Do you see what heights the discourse has climbed? How far it surpasses in greatness what was shown earlier in the Psalms?

CHAPTER 16. But even this is not the limit of the ascent to the heights for those who advance in virtue. For the psalm that follows this one in order is also found to surpass it in the grandeur of its contemplation. Again the title proclaims the crowned victor; again an inscribed pillar upon them testifies that such a victory is beyond human power. “For the end,” it says, “Do not destroy.” It has often been said that “the end” signifies victory, and there is no need to explain again in this discourse what is already known. But “Do not destroy,” this kindly saying, which goes beyond every extreme of forbearance, rises in this passage to a greater meaning. For who does not know that anyone at all is ready to do good to those who have shown no prior malice? Often, too, when some slight offence has occurred, the more magnanimous person bears the unpleasantness over small things, and when the time for kindness comes he is not deterred from treating well the one who caused him moderate grief; but the small-minded person, however trivial the provocation, unleashes his whole power of retaliation on the offender, seizing some opportunity to do him harm. So the wonder is not equal, even if the benefit happens to be the same, in the case of one who has suffered no prior wrong and of one who repays with kindness the person who first grieved him. For this reason, to show above all the incomparable and unrivalled forbearance of David, which very nearly imitates the impassibility of the divine nature itself, he sets beside it that wicked madness of Saul. For the saying “Do not destroy,” it says, which he inscribes as on a pillar for the memory of later generations, was spoken by David not when the tyrant was friendly toward him, but after those events had already happened, when Saul sent to his house to put him to death. You, lover of learning, are surely not unaware of the part

of the history that the title indicates: how, when Saul’s terror from the evil spirit had subsided, after holy David had calmed the turmoil of his affliction with the harp, Saul found his spear standing beside him and hurled it at his benefactor, aiming its point at him; but David, with divine help, slipped aside from the throw, and the spear struck deep and lodged in the wall. He ran out of the palace to his own house, hoping that the king’s anger would be changed by repentance. But Saul surrounded David’s house with guards and gave executioners orders to murder him, and David only just escaped danger by letting himself down through a window into the open air, unnoticed by the watch. Then he moved on, going now to one place, now to another, wandering in his helplessness among people he knew. And even so he was caught by Saul, who surrounded with his whole army the hill where David had taken refuge with his men. Since nightfall gave him a reprieve from death (for Saul had put off the slaughter of the man he was hunting until dawn), David came upon his enemy’s tent and found him relaxed in sleep on a bed. Not only did he restrain his own hand, which was perhaps eager to gratify his anger, but he also held back his shield-bearer, who was already bending over Saul to kill him (“I will strike,” he says, “and not need to strike twice”), with that great and celebrated cry, “Do not destroy,” addressed to the one who was hastening to destroy, as if to say, the man bent on our destruction. Nor is this the only marvel in the affair, that he grants life to the one who was doing everything against his life; it is also that David, having been anointed king and knowing that he could not attain that dignity unless Saul were out of the way, judged it better to suffer hardship through forbearance in private obscurity than to sate his anger against the one who had grieved him and so mount the throne. That is why, along with the merciful saying, he records the words “when Saul sent to David’s house to put him to death.” For it was not said at the time those things happened; rather, the text brings out the heightening of the marvel: the man who had suffered those things said these words. I think it superfluous now to insert into a discourse hurrying on to other matters what is asked about in the history: how, when the text has said that Saul struck David with the spear, the history adds that the spear went into the wall, and David [was saved?]; and that David himself is not found on his bed, but instead of him empty grave-clothes and goats’ liver. It was a custom among people of that time, as a way of warding off death, to take the sick man out of his bed and lay on the cot the garment put on the dead, together with goats’ liver. For it would be clear to the more diligent that the history is a prophecy of the Lord’s saving dispensation. There were demons in Saul the tyrant; these are driven out by the one anointed to

kingship, who used the instrument of the lyre to strike terror into them. But Saul, seized by the demons that dwelt with him, strikes with his spear the one who had shown through the lyre his power over the demons; yet the wall receives the blow instead of David, and he is kept safe. After this, the man plotted against by Saul is sought on his bed; and he is not found, but instead of him the bed holds empty grave-clothes and goats’ liver. The meaning of the riddles is quite plain, and so is what the sequence of the history points to. Through David the one from David is foretold, and the anointed one signifies Christ. The lyre is the human instrument, and the song from it is the Word made manifest to us through the one who became flesh, whose work is to abolish the frenzy caused by demons, so that the demons may no longer be the gods of the nations. But that king who has the demons within him, when the spirits retreat before the song, strikes with his spear the instrument tuned for this purpose (a spear is wood armed with iron); yet the wall receives the spear instead of him. By the wall we understand the earthly building, through which we come to understand the body, on which we see the wood and iron of the cross. But that David, the anointed one and king, is beyond suffering, for the Godhead does not come to be on the cross and in the nails. When we hear of Michal, the daughter of Saul, with whom David shared his life, let us not be [surprised?] [?], looking to what follows. For we know that God did not make death; rather, the king of wickedness, who deprived himself of life, became the father of death. For through the envy of the devil death entered, and death reigned from Adam until the law. The Apostle wants it no longer to reign in our mortal body. So the one who tasted death on behalf of all comes into the house of her who was born of the Saul we have understood, and she is Michal [?]. The meaning of this name is “kingdom,” because until then sin reigned over nature. Having come there, he himself goes out through a window. The window signifies the return to the light of the one who showed himself to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death. But his empty grave-clothes are seen on the bed. For the angel too says to those seeking the Lord in the tomb, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here; he has risen. See the place where he lay.” Those who were seeking the Lord saw the tomb in which he was buried empty of the body they sought; only the burial wrappings were in it. So we understand that the empty grave-clothes on David’s bed signify the resurrection of the Lord from the tomb, through which comes the true warding-off of our death. Since the wall that was pierced, which we took to stand for the body,

has no blood, so that the most essential of the things understood in the mystery, through which we were redeemed (I mean the blood), may not be left out, this is found in the empty grave-clothes. For of the internal organs the liver alone is the source and workshop of blood, and without it the substance of blood cannot be formed. If, then, the blood comes from the liver, and the liver is with the empty grave-clothes, blood too is not lacking in this warding-off of death that took place for human nature. Moreover, the species of the animal from which the liver was taken is set apart for sacrifices of atonement for sins. Not only that, but an animal of the same species is also taken for the Passover; and Moses says this animal must be used to send away the people’s sin, when it is divided for a twofold function: two goats are presented and lots are cast, and one is dedicated to God while the other is sent out into the wilderness for sin. For all these and similar reasons, then, the liver of this animal was taken to signify the blood through which the warding-off of death came for those mortally sick, through the resurrection of our Lord from the dead, which the empty tomb signifies.

But it is time to run briefly through the meaning of the psalm, which is as follows. The prophecy divides its speech. One part is addressed to God on our behalf, as common human nature is brought forward; the other is addressed to us by the one who took up suffering on our behalf. The words on our behalf are these: “Deliver me from my enemies, O God,” he says, “and redeem me from those who rise up against me. Rescue me from those who work lawlessness, and save me from men of blood, for they have hunted my soul”; and they attacked fiercely, though they had suffered no prior harm from us. For I committed no sin against them, nor has any lawless act been done by us to harm our enemies that might provoke them. Without lawlessness we ran our first course. “But see,” he says, “all things as they are. Look and attend to visit.” And do not, out of kindness, put off punishing the offenders. “For do not have pity,” he says, “on all who work lawlessness.” Then he shifts the speech to the higher person and speaks as from the one who heard the prayer: these enemies will return at evening. This means nothing other than that they will be driven together into the outer darkness, for evening is the beginning and mother of darkness. “And they will be hungry like a dog.” For those who have no provision for salvation must inevitably suffer the misery that comes from hunger for good things. So the rich man hungered in Hades, being bereft of the divine dew; and because he was unprepared for such a state, he burned in the flame. But it also says, “They will go around the city.” This seems to me to suggest something like the following meaning. Since everything useless and discarded, as far as the needs of the living are concerned, is thrown outside the city, whether a dead and rotting carcass or

foul-smelling dung, and it is around these that dogs are found, driven by the compulsion of hunger, living in the filth thrown out of the city, the text, teaching through this the difference between those who live in virtue and those who live in vice, conveys it by the riddle of the city. By “city” it means the seemly and well-ordered way of life founded by virtue; and what is outside the city denotes the vice seen in contrast to it, in which every rejection of the more refined life is a foul-smelling sin, found to be made up of the putrefaction of bodies and of filthy dung. So the inhabitant of the city, that great and precious thing, is the true human being, who has the character stamped on our nature from the beginning formed in him through his way of life. But whoever hangs about outside the city is a dog and not a human being. So it should be clear to everyone how dogs must be distinguished from those who are human by nature: not, I mean, by the shape of the body’s form, but by the difference in way of life. For the inhabitant of the virtuous city is truly a human being; but if someone devotes his zeal to foul-smelling licentiousness, or to the excremental greed which one might properly call dung, or to the other kinds of vice, wandering and creeping about outside the circuit of that city, he cries out against himself that he is a dog, his nature having been reshaped from the likeness to God into something dog-like. And by the dogs you surely understand the original dog, the flesh-eater and murderer, as the [?]

The rest of the psalm, too, describes the dog-like life. Instead of barking, it says, a kind of utterance comes from their mouth, and instead of fangs, a sword lies hidden in their lips, in these words: “See, they will utter with their mouth, and a sword is in their lips.” But these fearsome things are a laughing matter to those who have God within them. “For you, Lord,” he says, “will laugh them to scorn; but I will guard my strength for you.” And shortly after, he foretells the dispensation God has determined for his own creature. For he says: “Do not kill them, but bring them down” from the height of wickedness to the level, even ground of a life lived according to God [?]. This is just what the great Paul and John the Baptist did: in Paul, every high thing raised up against the knowledge of God was pulled down; and by John, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, every mountain and hill was brought low. From this we learn that human beings will not be annihilated, lest God’s work be rendered useless by being obliterated into nonexistence. Instead, sin will perish in their place and be reduced to nothing. “For the sin of their mouth,” he says, “and the word of their lips.” And pride, and cursing, and

lying will not exist in the wrath of the consummation. When these no longer exist [?], “They will know,” he says, “that God is Lord of Jacob and of the ends of the earth.” For once no wickedness at all is left, the Lord will surely be master of the ends of the earth, since the sin that now reigns over the many will have been taken out of the way. Then he takes up the same words again about those “who return at evening,” and are hungry like dogs, and go around the city, showing, I think, by repeating the words, that in either case, whether in evil or in what is better, people will be hereafter in the same state they are in now. For whoever now walks around in a circle through ungodliness, not living in the city nor keeping the human character in his own life, but turning into a beast by his choice and becoming a dog, will then also fall from the city above and be punished with hunger for good things. But the one who conquers his adversaries and goes forward (as the Psalmist says somewhere else) “from strength to strength,” passing from victory to victory, says, “I will sing of your strength, and in the morning I will rejoice in your mercy. For you have become my helper and my refuge,” and to you belongs the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

BY THE SAME AUTHOR: ON THE SIXTH PSALM, CONCERNING THE EIGHTH

Those who go from strength to strength, according to the prophetic blessing, and who set good ascents in their hearts, are led, whenever they grasp some good thought, by that thought to a higher one, through which the soul makes its ascent to the heights. So whoever is always straining toward what lies ahead will never cease from the good ascent, being always led through lofty thoughts to the understanding of those that lie still higher. I have said this, brothers, as I turn my mind to the sixth of the psalms and see the necessary sequence of their order: how after the psalm “For her who inherits,” the discourse “Concerning the Eighth” has been added for us. You are surely not unaware of the mystery of the Eighth. It is not fitting for anyone’s mind to be carried away to Jewish notions, as with those who bring down the grandeur of the mystery of the Eighth to the [unseemly?] parts of our body, the law of circumcision, and

…the purification after childbirth, and things of that kind, they say, are signified by the number of the Eighth. But we have learned from the great Paul that the law is spiritual. So even though this number occurs in the laws mentioned, which prescribe circumcision for the male and the sacrifice of purification for the woman, we neither reject the law nor take it in a lowly sense. We know that it is truly on the eighth day that the true circumcision takes place, performed with the knife of stone. By the stone that cuts away what is unclean we certainly understand the Rock itself, which is Christ, that is, the word of truth. And we know that the defiling flow of this life's affairs ceases at that time, when human life has been transformed into something more divine. To make clear to everyone what is meant in such matters, I will set out the argument more plainly, as far as I am able. In the first making of creation, the time of this life was completed in a single week of days. The making of the things that exist began with the first day, and the end of creation came with the seventh. "There was," Scripture says, "one day," on which the first things came to be; in the same way the second things came on the second day, and so on in order until everything was made by the sixth. The seventh, which was the end of creation, enclosed within itself the time that had stretched alongside the building of the world. No heaven has come into being since then, and no other part of the world has been added to those that came to be in the beginning. Creation stands by itself, remaining within its own measures, needing nothing added and suffering no loss. In the same way, no other time has come into being beyond the time that appeared together with the making of the world. The nature of time was bounded by the week of days. This is why, whenever we measure time by days, we begin from the first and close the count with the seventh, and then go back again to the first. We always measure out the whole extent of time by the cycle of weeks, until the things that move have passed away and the flowing motion has at last ceased. Then, as the Apostle says, the things that are no longer shaken will come, which change and alteration no longer touch, and that creation will remain always the same, in the same way, for the ages to come. In it the true circumcision of human nature takes place, in the stripping away of bodily life, and the true purification from the true filth. A human being's filth is sin, which is born together with human nature ("for in sins my mother conceived me"). Then he who made purification for our sins will cleanse it away entirely, consuming out of the nature of things everything that is bloody, filthy and uncircumcised. This is how we understand the law of the Eighth, which purifies and circumcises. When the time of weeks has ceased, an eighth day will come after the seventh. It is called eighth because it comes after the seventh,

but it no longer admits the succession of numbers within itself. It remains one forever and is never divided by the darkness of night. Another sun makes it, the one that shines out the true light. Once this sun has shone upon us, as the Apostle says, it no longer hides in its setting. It embraces all things with its power to give light, and gives the worthy a light that never ceases and is never followed by another. It even makes those who share in that light into other suns, as the Word says in the Gospel: "Then the righteous will shine like the sun." In the preceding psalm he spoke about the one who inherits. The inheritance is stored up for the worthy in the Eighth, and in it God's righteous judgment also takes place, giving each person what they deserve. So the Prophet did well to join the discourse on repentance to the mention of the Eighth. For who can call to mind the fearful judgment of Christ without being torn at once in his own conscience and gripped by fear and uncertainty? Even if he happens to know that his life has been better than most, he still looks to the strictness of the judgment, in which even the smallest oversights are examined. He is utterly terrified as he waits for fearful things, not knowing how the judgment will end for him. So, as if he had before his eyes the fearful punishments (that Gehenna and the dark fire, and the endless worm of conscience, which forever sucks at the soul through shame and renews its pains by the memory of a wicked life), he becomes a suppliant of God even now. He begs not to be handed over to that wrath to be convicted, and not to have the correction for his offenses brought upon him through that anger. For those who are condemned to the bitter correction of that fearful punishment think of the judgment as a work of wrath and anger. Therefore, as if he were already in the midst of the pains, he takes on the voices of those in anguish, to whom the punishment brought upon the ungodly seems to be wrath and anger. So he says: I will not wait for that wrath to expose my hidden deeds through fearful scourges; instead I will forestall by confession the compulsion that comes from that anger. Pain forces those who are scourged to bring the hidden things of their lawlessness into the open against their will. Free choice does the same thing of its own accord: it scourges and punishes itself through repentance and makes public the sin that lay concealed in hidden places. So, having said, "Do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor chasten me in your anger," he then takes refuge in mercy. He traces the cause of the evil not so much to choice as to the weakness of nature: I have fallen into evils; heal me with mercy, for I came to this passion out of weakness. And what is the weakness? My bones have been put out of joint and loosened from their fitting together. By bones he means the

sound and sober thoughts that hold the soul up: "Heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled." He explains the riddle of these words by what he adds to them: "My soul is greatly troubled." He says: Why then, Lord, do you put off the healing? Until when will you withhold your mercy? Do you not see how quickly human life comes to its end? By turning to my soul, forestall what must come to our life [?], so that death does not seize us and leave every remedy useless. For in death there will no longer be anyone who can heal, through remembrance of God, the sickness that evil has caused him. On earth confession has power, but in Hades it does not. Then it is as if someone asked: How do you call on mercy to heal your offenses? How have you won God's favor? He answers: "I have grown weary with my groaning, and I will wash out the bed of sin with the water of tears." Why these things? He says: Because my eye was troubled by wrath, and so I became old and wrinkled, since the wrath that my enemies stirred in me rotted my soul. If wrath alone causes so much fear in someone who has offended through it, how much more likely is it that people will despair of saving hope when their own lives show them guilty not only of the passions that come from wrath but also of everything that desire works, and greed, and pride, and ambition, and envy, and the rest of the swarm of human evils? This is why he turns his words against his enemies of every kind and says: "Depart from me, all you who work lawlessness." In the words that follow he shows the good hope of the success that repentance brings us. As soon as he had brought his words of repentance before God and become aware of God's kindness toward him, he makes the grace known and rejoices in the gift, saying: "The Lord has heard the voice of my supplication; the Lord has accepted my prayer." He wants the good that came to him from repentance to remain with him forever, so that his life will not need a second repentance. So he asks that his enemies be turned back, scourged with shame. For someone who has been put to shame when attempting evil will use that shame as a tutor so that he does not fall into the same things again, and he will keep away from anything like them in the time to come. This is the order of the good ascent. The fourth psalm distinguished the immaterial good from the bodily and more fleshly good. The fifth prayed for the inheritance of such a good. The sixth pointed to the time of the inheritance by mentioning the Eighth. The Eighth revealed the fear of the judgment. The judgment counseled us sinners to forestall the fearful things by repentance. Then repentance, brought before God in the right way,

announced the good news of what we gain from it, saying: "The Lord has heard the voice of the one who turns to him with tears." Once this has happened, the Prophet prays that hostile thoughts may be destroyed through shame, so that the good may remain with us unchanged in the time to come. A hostile and lawless thought cannot be put out in any other way unless shame brings about its destruction. Shame at a wicked life becomes a deep, fixed chasm, and by itself it walls a person off from his sin. So he says: "Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly confounded." Clearly these enemies are the ones of his own household, the ones that come out of the heart and defile a person. When they have quickly been turned back in shame, the hope of glory will take their place for us, a hope that does not end in shame, by the grace of the Lord, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.
